On meeting Anna Karenina — being, as he was, Alexey Alexandrovitch's enemy in government — he tried, like a shrewd man of the world, to be especially courteous to her, the wife of his enemy.

"'Nothing,'" he put in with a subtle smile, "that's the very best method. I told you long ago," he said, turning to Liza Merkalova, "that if you don't want to be bored, you mustn't think you're going to be bored. It's just the same as not being able to fall asleep when you're afraid of not being able to fall asleep. That's exactly what Anna Arkadyevna just said."
"I'd be very pleased if I had said it, because it's not only clever but also true," said Anna, smiling.
"No — do tell me, why is it one can't go to sleep, and one can't help being bored?"
"To sleep well one has to work, and to enjoy oneself one has to work too."
"And what am I supposed to work for, when my work is no use to anyone? I can't and won't deliberately fake it."

"You're incorrigible," said Stremov, not looking at her, and he turned back to Anna. Since he rarely met Anna, he could only say commonplaces — but he said those commonplaces, about when she was returning to Petersburg and how fond Countess Lidia Ivanovna was of her, in a tone that suggested he longed with his whole soul to please her, to show his regard for her, and even more than that.
Tushkevitch came in to announce that the others were waiting for the rest of the players to begin croquet.
"No, don't go, please don't," pleaded Liza Merkalova, hearing that Anna was going to leave. Stremov joined her appeals.

"It's too violent a transition," he said, "to go from this kind of company to old Madame Vrede. And besides, you'll only give her an opening for scandal-mongering, while here you stir nothing but very different feelings — feelings of the highest and most opposite kind," he said to her.

Anna paused for a moment, weighing it. This shrewd man's flattering words, the naive, childlike affection Liza Merkalova was showing her, the whole familiar social atmosphere — it was all so easy, and what lay ahead of her was so hard, that for a moment she hesitated whether to stay, whether to put off the painful moment of explanation a little longer. But remembering what was waiting for her alone at home, if she didn't come to some decision — remembering that gesture, terrible even in memory, when she had clutched her hair in both hands — she said goodbye and left.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: In spite of Vronsky's seemingly frivolous social life, he was a man who hated disorder. Early on, as a youth in the Corps of Pages, he had once experienced the humiliation of a refusal when, in a tight spot, he had tried to borrow money — and since then he had never put himself in that position again.

To keep his affairs in some kind of order, he used about five times a year (more or less often, depending on circumstances) to shut himself up alone and put everything into clear shape. He called this his day of reckoning, or _faire la lessive_.

Waking up the day after the races, Vronsky put on a white linen coat, and without shaving or taking a bath he spread his money, bills, and letters across the table and got to work. Petritsky, who knew he was in a foul mood on these occasions, woke up, saw his comrade at the writing-table, and dressed and slipped out quietly without getting in his way.

Every man who knows in minute detail the full complexity of the conditions he is surrounded by cannot help imagining that this complexity, and the difficulty of sorting it out, is something exceptional and personal — peculiar to himself — and never suspects that everyone else is surrounded by an equally tangled set of personal affairs. So it seemed to Vronsky. And not without some inner pride, and not without reason, he thought that any other man would long ago have come to grief or been forced into something dishonorable if he had found himself in such a tight position. But Vronsky felt that right now in particular it was essential to clarify and define his position if he wanted to avoid getting into trouble.

What Vronsky tackled first, as the easiest, was his money. Writing out all his debts on notepaper in his small hand, he added them up and found that they came to seventeen thousand and some odd hundreds, which he left off for the sake of clarity. Counting up his cash and his bank book, he found he had one thousand eight hundred roubles left, with nothing coming in before the New Year. Going over the list of debts again, Vronsky copied it out, sorting them into three classes. In the first class he put the debts that had to be paid at once, or for which he had to have the money ready so there could be no delay if payment were demanded. These came to about four thousand: one thousand five hundred for a horse, and two thousand five hundred as surety for a younger comrade, Venovsky, who had lost that sum to a cardsharper in Vronsky's presence. Vronsky had wanted to pay the money at the time (he had had the amount then), but Venovsky and Yashvin had insisted that they would pay, not Vronsky, who hadn't played. That much was all right, but Vronsky knew that in this dirty business — even though his only stake in it was a verbal promise to be Venovsky's surety — it was essential to have the two thousand five hundred roubles, so he could fling it at the swindler and have no more dealings with him. So for this first and most important category he needed four thousand roubles. The second class — eight thousand roubles — consisted of less urgent debts. These were mostly accounts connected with his race horses: the dealer in oats and hay, the English saddler, and so on. He would need to pay about two thousand roubles on those debts too in order to be quite free of worry. The last class of debts — to shops, to hotels, to his tailor — were not worth thinking about. So he needed at least six thousand roubles for current expenses, and he had only one thousand eight hundred. For a man with an income of one hundred thousand roubles, which was what everyone took Vronsky's income to be, debts like these should hardly have been embarrassing — but the truth was he was far from having one hundred thousand. His father's enormous fortune, which alone produced two hundred thousand a year, was still left undivided between the brothers. When the elder brother, weighed down with debts, had married Princess Varya Tchirkova, the penniless daughter of a Decembrist, Alexey had given up to his elder brother nearly the whole income from his father's estate, reserving for himself only twenty-five thousand a year out of it. Alexey had said to his brother at the time that this would be enough for him until he married — which he probably never would. And his brother, who commanded one of the most expensive regiments and had only just been married, could not refuse the gift. His mother, who had her own separate fortune, had been adding another twenty thousand a year to the twenty-five he had set aside, and Alexey had spent it all. Lately his mother, furious with him over his love affair and his leaving Moscow, had stopped sending him the money. As a result, Vronsky — who was used to a scale of forty-five thousand a year and had only received twenty thousand that year — found himself in trouble. He could not turn to his mother to get out of it. Her latest letter, received the day before, had especially infuriated him with its hints that she was perfectly ready to help him succeed in society and in the army, but not to support a life that was a scandal to all of decent society. His mother's attempt to buy him cut him to the quick and made him feel colder to her than ever. But he couldn't go back on the generous gesture once it had been made — even though he now felt, vaguely sensing certain possibilities ahead in his affair with Madame Karenina, that the generous gesture had been made carelessly, and that even unmarried he might need all hundred thousand of the income. But he couldn't undo it. He only had to remember his brother's wife, to remember how that dear, sweet Varya took every chance to remind him that she remembered his generosity and was grateful for it, to feel that taking the gift back was out of the question. It was as impossible as beating a woman, stealing, or lying. One thing only could and ought to be done, and Vronsky decided on it without an instant's hesitation: to borrow money from a money-lender — ten thousand roubles, a thing that presented no difficulty — to cut back his expenses across the board, and to sell his race horses. Having decided this, he immediately wrote a note to Rolandak, who had sent more than once with offers to buy horses from him. Then he sent for the Englishman and the money-lender, and divided what cash he had according to the bills he meant to pay. With that finished, he wrote a cold and cutting reply to his mother. Then he took out three notes from Anna out of his notebook, read them through again, burned them, and remembering their conversation the day before, sank into thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Vronsky's life was particularly happy in this: he had a code of principles that laid down with unfailing certainty what he ought and ought not to do. The code covered only a very small range of situations, but within that range the principles were never in doubt, and Vronsky, who never stepped outside it, had never had a moment's hesitation about doing what he was supposed to do. The principles laid down as fixed rules: that one must pay a card-sharper but need not pay one's tailor; that one must never lie to a man but may lie to a woman; that one must never cheat anyone but may cheat a husband; that one must never forgive an insult but may give one — and so on. These principles might not be reasonable or good, but they were unfailingly certain, and as long as he kept to them Vronsky felt that his heart was at peace and his head could stay up. Only quite recently, in connection with his affair with Anna, had Vronsky begun to feel that his code didn't fully cover every possible case, and to foresee in the future difficulties and dilemmas for which he could find no clear guide.
His present relation to Anna and to her husband seemed to him clear and simple. It was clearly and precisely defined in the code he lived by.

She was an honorable woman who had given him her love, and he loved her, and so in his eyes she was a woman entitled to the same respect as a lawful wife, or more. He would have had his hand cut off before he allowed himself by a word, by even a hint, to humiliate her, or to fall short of the fullest respect any woman could expect.

His attitude toward society was clear as well. Anyone might know, anyone might suspect — but no one was to dare speak of it. If anyone did, he was ready to force every speaker to be silent and to respect the nonexistent honor of the woman he loved.

His attitude toward the husband was the clearest of all. From the moment Anna had loved Vronsky, he had regarded his own right over her as the one thing beyond question. The husband was simply a superfluous, tiresome presence. No doubt the man was in a pitiable position — but how could that be helped? The one right the husband had was to demand satisfaction with a weapon in his hand, and Vronsky was prepared for that at any moment.

But lately a new kind of inner connection had grown up between him and her, one whose vagueness frightened Vronsky. Only the day before she had told him she was pregnant. And he felt that this fact, and what she expected of him in response to it, called for something not fully spelled out in the code by which he had so far steered his life. He had indeed been caught off guard, and in the first moment when she spoke to him about her position, his heart had urged him to beg her to leave her husband. He had said it — but now, thinking it over, he saw clearly that it would be better to find a way to avoid that; and at the same time, even as he was telling himself this, he was afraid it might be wrong.

"If I told her to leave her husband, that would mean joining her life to mine; am I ready for that? How am I supposed to take her away now, with no money? Suppose I could arrange it... But how can I take her away while I'm still in the service? If I say it — I have to be prepared to do it, that is, I have to have the money and to retire from the army."
And he fell into thought. The question of whether to retire from the service or not led him to the other and perhaps the chief, though hidden, interest of his life — one no one but he knew about.

Ambition was the old dream of his youth and childhood, a dream he didn't even admit to himself, although it was so strong that this passion was now even doing battle with his love. His first steps in society and in the service had been successful, but two years before he had made a serious mistake. Eager to show his independence and get ahead, he had refused a post that was offered to him, hoping that the refusal would make him more valuable; but as it turned out, he had been too bold, and was passed over. And having, whether he liked it or not, taken on the position of an independent man, he had carried it off with great tact and good sense, behaving as if he held nothing against anyone, considered himself slighted in no way, and cared for nothing but to be left alone since he was enjoying himself. In reality he had stopped enjoying himself as far back as the year before, when he had gone away to Moscow. He felt that this independent posture of a man who might have done anything but cared to do nothing was already beginning to pall, that many people were starting to think he wasn't actually capable of anything beyond being a straightforward, good-natured fellow. His affair with Madame Karenina, by causing such a sensation and drawing such general attention, had given him a fresh distinction that quieted the gnawing worm of ambition for a while — but a week ago that worm had been stirred up again with new force. The friend of his childhood, a man from the same set, the same coterie, his comrade in the Corps of Pages, Serpuhovskoy, who had left school with him and had been his rival in class, in gymnastics, in their pranks and their dreams of glory, had just returned from Central Asia, where he had gained two steps in rank and an order rarely given to generals so young.

As soon as he arrived in Petersburg, people started talking about him as a newly risen star of the first magnitude. A schoolmate of Vronsky's, the same age as he was, he was now a general, expecting a command that might shape the course of political events; while Vronsky, however independent, brilliant, and beloved by a charming woman, was simply a cavalry captain whose independence everyone was happy to indulge. "Of course I don't envy Serpuhovskoy and never could; but his advancement shows me that all one has to do is watch one's chance, and a man like me may have a career made very quickly. Three years ago he was in exactly the position I'm in. If I retire, I burn my ships. If I stay in the army, I lose nothing. She herself said she didn't want to change her position. And with her love I can't envy Serpuhovskoy." And slowly twirling his mustaches, he got up from the table and walked around the room. His eyes were shining particularly brightly, and he was in that confident, calm, and contented frame of mind which always came over him after he had thoroughly faced his situation. Everything was straight and clear, just as after his previous days of reckoning. He shaved, took a cold bath, dressed, and went out.

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: "We've come to fetch you. Your _lessive_ went on quite a while today," said Petritsky. "So — is it over?"

"It's over," Vronsky answered, smiling only with his eyes and twirling the ends of his mustaches as carefully as if, after the perfect order he had just brought to his affairs, any too bold or sudden movement might upset it.
"You always look as though you'd just come out of the bath afterward," said Petritsky. "I've come from Gritsky's" (that was what they called the colonel); "they're expecting you."
Vronsky, without answering, looked at his comrade, his mind on something else.
"Yes — is that music coming from his place?" he said, listening to the familiar sounds of polkas and waltzes drifting over. "What's the party for?"
"Serpuhovskoy has come."
"Aha!" said Vronsky. "I didn't know."
The smile in his eyes glinted brighter than ever.

Having decided once and for all that he was happy in his love, that he was sacrificing his ambition to it — having, in any case, taken up that position — Vronsky was incapable either of envying Serpuhovskoy or of being hurt that he hadn't come to him first on returning to the regiment. Serpuhovskoy was a good friend, and he was delighted he had come.
"Oh, I'm very glad!"

The colonel, Demin, had taken a large country house. The whole party was on the wide lower balcony. In the courtyard the first things to catch Vronsky's eye were a band of singers in white linen coats, standing by a barrel of vodka, and the robust, good-humored figure of the colonel surrounded by officers. He had walked out as far as the first step of the balcony and was shouting at full volume across the band — which was playing Offenbach's quadrille — waving his arms and giving orders to a few soldiers standing off to one side. A group of soldiers, a quartermaster, and several subalterns came up to the balcony along with Vronsky. The colonel went back to the table, came out again onto the steps with a tumbler in his hand, and proposed the toast: "To the health of our former comrade, the gallant general, Prince Serpuhovskoy. Hurrah!"
Behind the colonel came Serpuhovskoy, stepping out onto the steps smiling, glass in hand.

"You only get younger, Bondarenko," he said to the rosy-cheeked, smart-looking quartermaster standing just in front of him — a man still youngish-looking, though he was doing his second term of service.

It had been three years since Vronsky had seen Serpuhovskoy. He looked more robust, had let his whiskers grow, but was still the same graceful figure, whose face and form were even more striking for their softness and nobility than for their beauty. The only change Vronsky noticed in him was that subdued, steady radiance of contentment that settles on the faces of men who are successful and sure that their success is acknowledged by everyone. Vronsky knew that radiant air, and spotted it in Serpuhovskoy at once.

Coming down the steps, Serpuhovskoy caught sight of Vronsky. A smile of pleasure lit up his face. He tossed his head back and waved the glass in his hand at Vronsky in greeting, showing him by the gesture that he couldn't come over before dealing with the quartermaster, who was standing with his lips already pushed forward to be kissed.
"Here he is!" the colonel shouted. "Yashvin told me you were in one of your gloomy moods."
Serpuhovskoy kissed the moist, fresh lips of the dashing-looking quartermaster, wiped his mouth with his handkerchief, and came over to Vronsky.
"How glad I am!" he said, squeezing his hand and pulling him aside.
"You look after him," the colonel shouted to Yashvin, pointing at Vronsky, and went down to the soldiers.
"Why weren't you at the races yesterday? I'd expected to see you there," said Vronsky, studying Serpuhovskoy.

"I did go, but late. Sorry about that," he added, and turned to the adjutant: "Please divide this up from me — however much it comes to per man." And he hurriedly took notes for three hundred roubles out of his pocketbook, blushing slightly.
"Vronsky! Want something to eat or drink?" Yashvin asked. "Hey, something for the count to eat! Ah, here it is — have a glass!"

The party at the colonel's went on for a long time. There was a great deal of drinking. They tossed Serpuhovskoy in the air and caught him again several times. Then they did the same to the colonel. Then, to the accompaniment of the band, the colonel himself danced with Petritsky. Then the colonel, who was starting to flag, sat down on a bench in the courtyard and began explaining to Yashvin the superiority of Russia over Prussia, especially in cavalry charges, and the revelry lulled for a moment. Serpuhovskoy went into the house to the bathroom to wash his hands and found Vronsky there; Vronsky was dousing his head with water. He had taken off his coat and stuck his sunburned, hairy neck under the tap, rubbing it and his head with his hands. When he was done, Vronsky sat down beside Serpuhovskoy. They both took seats on a lounge in the bathroom, and a conversation began that was very interesting to both of them.
"I've always heard about you through my wife," said Serpuhovskoy. "I'm glad you've been seeing her pretty often."

"She's friends with Varya, and they're the only women in Petersburg I care to see," Vronsky answered, smiling. He smiled because he could see what direction the conversation was about to take, and he was glad of it.
"The only ones?" Serpuhovskoy asked back, smiling.

"Yes — and I'd been hearing news of you, and not only through your wife," said Vronsky, cutting off the hint with a stern look. "I was delighted to hear of your success, though not at all surprised. I'd expected even more."
Serpuhovskoy smiled. Such an opinion of him was obviously pleasing, and he didn't see the point of hiding it.
"Well — I, on the contrary, had expected less; I'll admit that honestly. But I'm glad, very glad. I'm ambitious; that's my weakness, and I own up to it."
"Perhaps you wouldn't own up to it if you hadn't succeeded," said Vronsky.

"I don't suppose so," said Serpuhovskoy, smiling again. "I won't go as far as saying life wouldn't be worth living without it, but it would be dull. Of course I may be wrong, but I do think I have a certain talent for the line I've chosen, and that any power that comes into my hands, if it does, will be better there than in the hands of plenty of men I know," said Serpuhovskoy, with the radiant consciousness of success. "And so the closer I get to it, the better pleased I am."
"Maybe that's true for you, but not for everyone. I used to think the same way, but here I am, and I find life worth living for more than just that."

"There it is! Here it comes!" said Serpuhovskoy, laughing. "Ever since I heard about you, about your refusal, I began... Of course, I approved of what you did. But there are ways of doing everything. I think your action was good in itself, but you didn't go about it quite the way you should have."
"What's done is done, and you know I never go back on what I've done. Besides, I'm quite well off as I am."

"Quite well off — for now. But you're not satisfied with that. I wouldn't say this to your brother. He's a nice child, like our host here. Listen to him go!" he added, hearing the roar of "hurrah!" — "and he's happy, but that doesn't satisfy you."
"I didn't say it did."
"Yes, but that's not the only thing. Men like you are needed."
"By whom?"
"By whom? By society, by Russia. Russia needs men; she needs a party — otherwise everything goes, and will go, to the dogs."
"What do you mean? Bertenev's party against the Russian communists?"

"No," said Serpuhovskoy, frowning in annoyance at being suspected of anything so absurd. "_Tout ça est une blague_. That's always been around and always will be. There are no communists. But scheming people have to invent a noxious, dangerous party. It's an old trick. No — what's needed is a powerful party of independent men like you and me."
"But why?" Vronsky named several men currently in power. "Why aren't they independent men?"

"Simply because they don't have, or never had from birth, an independent fortune; they haven't had a name, they haven't been close to the sun and center the way we have. They can be bought either with money or with favor. And they have to find themselves a foothold by inventing some policy. So they come up with some notion, some program they don't really believe in, that does damage; and the whole policy is really just a means to a government house and so much income. _Cela n'est pas plus fin que ça_, once you get a glimpse of their cards. I may be inferior to them, perhaps stupider — though I don't see why I should be. But you and I do have one decisive advantage over them, in being harder to buy. And such men are needed now more than ever."

Vronsky listened attentively, but it wasn't so much the content of the words that interested him as Serpuhovskoy's attitude — already contemplating a struggle with the powers that be, already with his likes and dislikes set out in that higher world, while Vronsky's own interest in the governing sphere went no further than the interests of his regiment. Vronsky also felt how powerful Serpuhovskoy might become through his unmistakable gift for thinking things through and grasping situations, through his intelligence and his way with words, qualities he rarely encountered in the world he moved in. And, ashamed as he was of the feeling, he felt envious.
"Still, I lack the one thing that matters most for that," he answered; "I don't want power. I did once — but it's gone."
"Forgive me, but that isn't true," Serpuhovskoy said, smiling.
"Yes — it is true, it is true... now!" Vronsky added, to be honest.
"Yes, it's true now, that's a separate matter; but this _now_ won't last forever."
"Perhaps," Vronsky answered.

"You say _perhaps_," Serpuhovskoy went on, as if reading his thoughts, "but I say _for certain_. And that's why I wanted to see you. Your action was just what it should have been. I see that, but you shouldn't keep it up. All I'm asking is that you give me _carte blanche_. I'm not offering my protection... though, after all, why shouldn't I protect you? You've protected me often enough. I'd hope our friendship rises above that sort of thing. Yes," he said, smiling at him as tenderly as a woman, "give me _carte blanche_, retire from the regiment, and I'll draw you up by degrees."
"But you have to understand that I want nothing," said Vronsky, "except that everything should stay as it is."
Serpuhovskoy got up and stood facing him.

"You say everything should stay as it is. I understand what that means. But listen: we're the same age, and you've probably known more women than I have." Serpuhovskoy's smile and gestures told Vronsky he needn't be uneasy — that he would be gentle and careful in touching the sore spot. "But I'm married, and believe me, in getting to know thoroughly one's own wife, if one loves her, as someone has said, one comes to know all women better than if one had known thousands of them."
"We're coming, right away!" Vronsky shouted to an officer who looked into the room and called them to the colonel.
Vronsky was now longing to hear Serpuhovskoy out, to know what he was going to say to him.

"And here's my opinion for you. Women are the chief stumbling block in a man's career. It's hard to love a woman and do anything else. There's only one way to have love conveniently without its getting in the way — and that's marriage. How am I to put it?" said Serpuhovskoy, who loved analogies. "Wait a minute, wait a minute! Yes — just as you can only carry a _fardeau_ and still use your hands when the _fardeau_ is strapped to your back, and that's marriage. That's what I felt once I was married. My hands were suddenly set free. But to lug that _fardeau_ around without marriage, your hands will always be so full that you can't do anything else. Look at Mazankov, at Krupov. They've ruined their careers for the sake of women."
"What women, though!" said Vronsky, recalling the Frenchwoman and the actress the two men he'd named were involved with.
"The more firmly the woman is established in society, the worse it is. It's much the same as — not just carrying the _fardeau_ in your arms — but tearing it away from someone else."
"You've never loved," Vronsky said softly, looking straight ahead and thinking of Anna.
"Perhaps. But remember what I've said to you. And one more thing — women are all more materialistic than men. We make something enormous out of love, but they're always _terre-à-terre_."
"Right away, right away!" he called to a footman who came in. But the footman hadn't come to call them again, as he had assumed. The footman was bringing Vronsky a note.
"A man brought it from Princess Tverskaya."
Vronsky opened the letter and went crimson.
"My head's started to ache; I'm going home," he said to Serpuhovskoy.
"Oh, goodbye then. So — you give me _carte blanche?_"
"We'll talk about it later; I'll look you up in Petersburg."

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: It was already six o'clock. To get there fast — and without taking his own horses, which everyone in town would recognize — Vronsky climbed into Yashvin's hired fly and told the driver to push the pace. It was a roomy, old-fashioned fly with seats for four. He sank into one corner, stretched his legs across to the front seat, and fell into thought.

A vague sense that his affairs had been put in order, a vague memory of Serpuhovskoy's friendliness and flattery — Serpuhovskoy, who had treated him as a man the country needed — and, above everything, the anticipation of the meeting ahead of him: all of it blended into a single, joyful feeling of being alive. The feeling was so strong he found himself smiling. He let his legs drop, crossed one knee over the other, took the calf in his hand, and felt the springy muscle where it had been grazed in his fall the day before. Then he leaned back and drew several deep breaths.

"I'm happy, very happy!" he said to himself. He had often felt this kind of physical joy in his own body before, but he had never been so fond of himself, of his own body, as he was now. He liked the slight ache in his strong leg; he liked the muscular sensation of his chest moving as he breathed. The bright, cold August day that had made Anna feel so hopeless struck him as keenly invigorating, refreshing his face and neck — which still tingled from the cold water he had splashed on himself. The scent of brilliantine on his whiskers seemed especially pleasant in the fresh air. Everything he saw through the carriage window — everything in that cold, pure air, in the pale light of the sunset — was as fresh and gay and strong as he was: the roofs of the houses gleaming in the sunset, the sharp edges of fences and the corners of buildings, the figures of passers-by, the carriages he met now and then, the still green of trees and grass, the fields with their evenly drawn potato furrows, and the slanting shadows that fell from the houses and trees and bushes — even from the rows of potatoes. The whole scene shone like a pretty landscape just painted and freshly varnished.

"On, on!" he called to the driver, leaning his head out of the window. He pulled a three-rouble note from his pocket and handed it over as the man looked back. The driver fumbled with something at the lamp, the whip cracked, and the carriage rolled swiftly along the smooth highroad.

"I want nothing — nothing but this happiness," he thought, staring at the bone bell-button in the space between the windows and picturing Anna exactly as he had seen her last. "And the longer this goes on, the more I love her. Here's the garden of the Vrede Villa. Where will she be? Where? How? Why did she choose this place to meet me, and why does she write to me through Betsy's letter?" — questions he was only now wondering about for the first time. But there was no time left for wondering. He called to the driver to stop before the avenue, opened the door, jumped out of the moving carriage, and walked up the avenue toward the house. The avenue was empty, but glancing to the right he caught sight of her. Her face was hidden by a veil, but his eyes drank in the way of walking that was hers and no one else's — the slope of the shoulders, the set of the head — and at once a kind of electric shock ran through him. He felt himself with renewed force, from the springy motion of his legs to the working of his lungs, and something made his lips twitch.
When she reached him, she pressed his hand tightly.
"You're not angry that I sent for you? I absolutely had to see you," she said. The serious, set line of her lips, visible under the veil, changed his mood at once.
"Angry — me! But how did you get here? Where did you come from?"
"Never mind," she said, laying her hand on his. "Come — I have to talk to you."

He understood that something had happened, and that this would not be a happy meeting. In her presence his will dissolved: without even knowing what was upsetting her, he felt the same distress passing into him unconsciously.
"What is it? What?" he asked, pressing her hand against his elbow and searching her face for her thoughts.
She walked on a few paces in silence, gathering her courage; then she suddenly stopped.

"I didn't tell you yesterday," she began, breathing quickly and painfully, "that when I came home with Alexey Alexandrovitch I told him everything... told him I couldn't be his wife, that... and told him everything."
He listened, his whole body unconsciously bending toward her as if to ease the weight of her position. But the moment she said it, he straightened up, and a proud, hard expression came over his face.

"Yes, yes — that's better, a thousand times better. I know how painful it was for you," he said. But she wasn't listening to his words. She was reading his thoughts from his face. She couldn't guess that the expression came from the first idea that had occurred to Vronsky — that a duel was now inevitable. A duel had never crossed her mind, and so she read his momentary hardness in a different way.

When she had received her husband's letter, she had known in the bottom of her heart that everything would go on as before — that she wouldn't have the strength of will to give up her position, abandon her son, and join her lover. The morning at Princess Tverskaya's had only confirmed it. Still, this meeting mattered to her enormously. She hoped it would transform her position and save her. If on hearing the news he said to her firmly, passionately, without an instant's hesitation, "Throw it all up and come with me!" — then she would give up her son and go away with him. But the news had not produced in him what she had hoped for; he simply looked as though he were nursing some affront.
"It wasn't in the least painful for me. It happened on its own," she said irritably. "And look...." She pulled her husband's letter out of her glove.

"I understand, I understand," he interrupted, taking the letter without reading it, trying to soothe her. "The one thing I longed for, the one thing I prayed for, was to put an end to this situation, so I could devote my life to your happiness."
"Why are you telling me that?" she said. "Do you think I can doubt it? If I doubted...."
"Who's that coming?" Vronsky said suddenly, pointing at two ladies walking toward them. "They may know us!" He turned aside hurriedly, pulling her with him into a side path.

"Oh, what does it matter!" she said. Her lips were trembling. And he imagined her eyes were looking at him with a strange fury from under the veil. "I tell you that's not the point — I can't doubt that. But look at what he writes me. Read it." She stopped again.

Just as in the first moment when he had heard of her rupture with her husband, Vronsky, on reading the letter, was carried away without realizing it by the natural reaction his relationship to the betrayed husband stirred in him. Holding the letter in his hands now, he couldn't help picturing the challenge he would probably find waiting for him at home today or tomorrow — and the duel itself, in which, with the same cold and haughty expression his face wore at this moment, he would stand ready for the injured husband's shot after firing into the air himself. And in that same instant, the thought flashed through his mind of what Serpuhovskoy had just said to him, of what he himself had been thinking that morning — that it was better not to tie himself down — and he knew this was a thought he could not share with her.

When he had finished reading, he raised his eyes to her, and there was no resolve in them. She saw at once that he had already been turning this over in his own mind. She knew that whatever he might say to her, he wouldn't say everything he was thinking. And she knew her last hope had failed. This was not what she had been counting on.
"You see the sort of man he is," she said, her voice shaking. "He...."

"Forgive me, but I'm glad of it," Vronsky interrupted. "For God's sake, let me finish!" he added, his eyes begging her to give him time to explain. "I'm glad, because things can't — they simply can't — stay the way he supposes they will."
"Why can't they?" Anna said, holding back her tears, clearly attaching no weight to anything he said. She felt her fate was sealed.
Vronsky meant that after the duel — which he considered unavoidable — things couldn't continue as before, but what came out was something else.
"It can't go on. I hope that now you'll leave him. I hope" — he was flustered, and reddened — "that you'll let me arrange our life and plan it. Tomorrow...." he was beginning.
She did not let him go on.
"But my child!" she cried. "Look what he writes! I'd have to leave him, and I can't and won't do that."
"But for God's sake — which is better? Leave your child, or keep up this degrading position?"
"To whom is it degrading?"
"To everyone, and most of all to you."

"You say degrading.... Don't say that. Those words have no meaning for me," she said with a trembling voice. She did not want him now to say anything untrue. All she had left was his love, and she wanted to love him. "Don't you see that from the day I loved you everything has changed for me? For me there is one thing, and one thing only — your love. If that is mine, I feel so lifted up, so strong, that nothing can humiliate me. I am proud of my position, because... proud of being... proud...." She couldn't say what she was proud of. Tears of shame and despair choked her voice. She stopped and sobbed.

He too felt something swelling in his throat and twitching at his nose, and for the first time in his life he felt on the verge of tears. He couldn't have said exactly what touched him so. He was sorry for her, and he felt he could not help her, and along with that he knew he was the cause of her misery, and that he had done something wrong.
"Is a divorce out of the question?" he asked weakly. She shook her head without answering. "Couldn't you take your son and still leave him?"
"Yes — but it all depends on him. I have to go to him now," she said shortly. Her presentiment that everything would simply continue as before had not deceived her.
"I'll be in Petersburg on Tuesday, and everything can be settled."
"Yes," she said. "But let's not talk about it anymore."
Anna's carriage, which she had sent away and ordered to come back to the small gate of the Vrede garden, drove up. Anna said goodbye to Vronsky and drove home.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: On Monday the Commission of the 2nd of June held its usual sitting. Alexey Alexandrovitch walked into the hall, greeted the members and the president as he always did, and took his seat, laying his hand on the papers already arranged in front of him. Among them were the necessary documents and a rough draft of the speech he meant to deliver. But he did not really need any of it. He remembered every point and saw no reason to rehearse mentally what he would say. He knew that when the moment came, and when he saw his enemy across from him studiously trying to look indifferent, the speech would flow of itself better than he could prepare it now. He felt that what he was about to say carried such weight that every word would tell. While the routine report was read, he kept the most harmless, inoffensive air. No one watching his white hands, with their swollen veins and long fingers gently stroking the edges of the white paper, or the air of weariness with which his head tilted to one side, would have suspected that in a few minutes a torrent of words would burst from his lips — a flood that would raise a storm, set the members shouting and attacking one another, and force the president to call for order. When the report ended, Alexey Alexandrovitch announced in his quiet, refined voice that he had several points to bring before the meeting concerning the Commission for the Reorganization of the Native Tribes. Every eye turned to him. He cleared his throat, and, instead of looking at his opponent, fixed his eyes — as he always did while speaking — on the first person sitting opposite him, an inoffensive little old man who had never had a single opinion in the Commission, and began to lay out his views. When he reached the point about the fundamental and radical law, his opponent jumped up and started to protest. Stremov, also a member of the Commission and stung to the quick, began defending himself, and the sitting turned stormy; but Alexey Alexandrovitch triumphed. His motion was carried, three new commissions were appointed, and the next day a certain Petersburg circle talked of nothing but the sitting. Alexey Alexandrovitch's success had been even greater than he had expected.

The next morning, Tuesday, Alexey Alexandrovitch woke remembering with pleasure his triumph of the previous day, and he couldn't help smiling — though he tried to look indifferent — when the chief secretary of his department, eager to flatter him, passed on the rumors that had reached him about what had happened in the Commission.

Absorbed in business with the chief secretary, Alexey Alexandrovitch had completely forgotten that it was Tuesday, the day he had fixed for Anna Arkadyevna's return, and he was startled and irritated when a servant came in to tell him she had arrived.

Anna had reached Petersburg early that morning; the carriage had been sent to meet her in accordance with her telegram, so Alexey Alexandrovitch could have known of her arrival. But when she came in, he did not go out to meet her. She was told he hadn't yet gone out, but was busy with his secretary. She sent word that she had come, went to her own room, and busied herself sorting her things, expecting him to come to her. But an hour went by, and he did not come. She went into the dining-room on the pretext of giving some orders, and spoke loudly on purpose, hoping he would come out to her; but he did not, though she heard him go to the door of his study as he saw the chief secretary off. She knew he usually left quickly for his office, and she wanted to see him before he did, so that the terms between them could be made clear.

She walked across the drawing-room and went straight to him. When she entered his study he was in his official uniform, plainly ready to go out, sitting at a small table with his elbows on it, staring dejectedly in front of him. She saw him before he saw her, and she could tell he was thinking of her.

When he saw her, he was about to rise, then changed his mind; then his face flushed a deep red — something Anna had never seen before. He got up quickly and went to meet her, not looking at her eyes but at a point above them, at her forehead and hair. He came up to her, took her hand, and asked her to sit down.

"I'm very glad you've come," he said, sitting down beside her, and clearly wanting to say something he stammered. Several times he tried to begin and stopped. Although she had prepared herself to despise and reproach him during the meeting, she didn't know what to say, and she felt sorry for him. So the silence stretched on. "Is Seryozha quite well?" he said, and without waiting for an answer added: "I shan't be dining at home today, and I have to go out directly."
"I had thought of going to Moscow," she said.
"No, you were quite, quite right to come," he said, and fell silent again.
Seeing he was incapable of starting the conversation, she began it herself.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch," she said, looking at him and not dropping her eyes under his steady stare at her hair, "I'm a guilty woman, I'm a bad woman, but I am the same as I was, as I told you then, and I have come to tell you that I can change nothing."

"I have asked you no question about that," he said, suddenly, decisively, looking her straight in the face with hatred. "That was what I had supposed." Anger seemed to give him back full command of all his faculties. "But as I told you then, and have written to you," he went on in a thin, shrill voice, "I repeat now: I am not obliged to know this. I ignore it. Not all wives are as kind as you, so quick to bring such pleasant news to their husbands." He emphasized the word "pleasant." "I shall continue to ignore it as long as the world knows nothing of it, as long as my name is not disgraced. So I simply inform you that our relations must be just as they have always been, and that only in the event of your compromising me will I be obliged to take steps to protect my honor."
"But our relations cannot be the same as always," Anna began in a timid voice, looking at him in dismay.

Once again seeing his composed gestures and hearing that shrill, childish, sarcastic voice, her revulsion for him snuffed out her pity, and she felt only afraid — but at all costs she meant to make her position clear.
"I cannot be your wife while I...." she began.
He laughed a cold, malignant laugh.

"I suppose the manner of life you have chosen is reflected in your ideas. I have too much respect — or contempt — or both... I respect your past and despise your present... so that the interpretation you put on my words was far from what I meant."
Anna sighed and bowed her head.

"Though I really fail to see how, with the independence you display" — he was warming to it now — "announcing your infidelity to your husband and apparently seeing nothing improper in it, you can find anything improper in fulfilling a wife's duties toward her husband."
"Alexey Alexandrovitch! What is it you want of me?"

"I want you not to meet that man here, and to conduct yourself so that neither the world nor the servants can reproach you... that you not see him. That isn't much, I think. And in return you will have all the privileges of a faithful wife without fulfilling her duties. That's all I have to say to you. Now I must go. I'm not dining at home." He got up and moved toward the door.
Anna got up too. He bowed in silence and let her pass before him.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: The night Levin had spent on the haycock did not pass without leaving its mark. The way he had been running his estate revolted him; it had lost all its appeal. In spite of the magnificent harvest, there had never been — or at least it seemed to him there had never been — so many obstacles and so many quarrels between him and the peasants as that year, and the root of these failures and this hostility was now completely clear to him. The pleasure he had taken in the work itself, the closeness with the peasants that grew out of it, the envy he felt for them and their way of life, the desire to live that way — which that night had been not a daydream but a definite intention, the carrying out of which he had worked through in detail — all of it had so changed his view of the farming he had been doing that he could no longer take his old interest in it, and could not help seeing the ugly relation between himself and the workers that lay underneath. The herd of improved cows like Pava, the whole land plowed and enriched, the nine level fields surrounded by hedges, the two hundred and forty acres heavily manured, the seed sown in drills, and all the rest of it — all of it would have been splendid if only the work had been done for themselves, or for themselves and comrades who shared their feelings. But now he saw clearly (his work on a book about agriculture, in which the laborer was to have been the chief element of husbandry, helped him greatly here) that the kind of farming he was carrying on was nothing but a cruel, stubborn struggle between him and his workers, with on one side — his side — a constant intense effort to remake everything along lines he thought better, and on the other side, the natural order of things. And in this struggle, with enormous expenditure of effort on his side and no effort and not even any intention on the other, he saw that all that was achieved was that the work pleased neither side, and that splendid tools, splendid livestock and land were spoiled to no one's benefit. Worst of all, the energy thrown into this work wasn't merely wasted. Now that the meaning of the system had become clear to him, he couldn't help feeling that the very aim of his energy was unworthy. What was the struggle actually about? He was struggling for every farthing of his share (and he had to — relax for a moment, and he wouldn't have had the money to pay his laborers' wages), while they were only struggling to be allowed to do their work easily and pleasantly — that is, as they were used to doing it. It was in his interests for every laborer to work as hard as possible and stay alert, so as not to break the winnowing machines, the horse rakes, the threshing machines, and to pay attention to what he was doing. What the laborer wanted was to work as pleasantly as possible, with rests, and above all carelessly and heedlessly, without thinking. Levin saw this at every step that summer. He sent the men to mow clover for hay, picking out the worst patches where the clover was overgrown with grass and weeds and useless for seed; again and again they mowed the best acres of clover, justifying themselves with the claim that the bailiff had told them to, and trying to reassure him that it would make splendid hay. But he knew they had done it because those acres were so much easier to mow. He sent out a hay machine for pitching the hay — it broke at the first row because it was dull work for a peasant to sit on the seat in front with the great wings waving above him. And he was told, "Don't trouble yourself, your honor — the womenfolk will pitch it quick enough." The plows were practically useless, because it never occurred to the laborer to raise the share when turning the plow; forcing it around, he strained the horses and tore up the ground, and Levin was begged not to mind. The horses were allowed to wander into the wheat because not a single laborer would agree to be night-watchman, and in spite of orders, the laborers insisted on taking turns at night duty, and Ivan, after working all day, fell asleep, and was very repentant about his lapse, saying, "Do what you will with me, your honor."

They killed three of his best calves by letting them into the clover aftermath without watching their drinking, and nothing would convince the men they had been bloated by the clover; they offered him the consolation that one of his neighbors had lost a hundred and twelve head of cattle in three days. None of this happened because anyone bore Levin or his farm ill will; on the contrary, he knew they liked him, considered him a simple gentleman (their highest praise). It happened simply because all they wanted was to work merrily and carelessly, and his interests were not only foreign and incomprehensible to them but in fatal conflict with their most legitimate claims. Levin had long felt dissatisfied with his own position with regard to the land. He saw where his boat was leaking, but he didn't look for the leak — perhaps he was deceiving himself on purpose. (If he lost faith in his work, nothing would be left to him.) But now he could no longer keep up the deception. Farming the land as he had been doing it had become not just unattractive but revolting to him, and he could take no further interest in it.

Added to all this was the presence, only twenty-five miles away, of Kitty Shtcherbatskaya — whom he longed to see and couldn't see. Darya Alexandrovna Oblonskaya had invited him, when he was over there, to come — to come with the aim of renewing his offer to her sister, who, Dolly hinted, would accept him now. Levin himself had felt, on seeing Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, that he had never stopped loving her; but he could not go to the Oblonskys' knowing she was there. The fact that he had made her an offer and she had refused him had set an insurmountable barrier between them. "I can't ask her to be my wife simply because she can't be the wife of the man she wanted to marry," he told himself. The thought made him feel cold and hostile toward her. "I wouldn't be able to talk to her without a feeling of reproach; I couldn't look at her without resentment; and she'll only hate me all the more for it, as she's bound to. And besides — how can I now, after what Darya Alexandrovna told me, go to see them? Can I keep from showing that I know what she told me? And go magnanimously to forgive her, to take pity on her? Put on a show in front of her of forgiving and condescending to grant her my love?... What possessed Darya Alexandrovna to tell me that? By chance I might have seen her, and then everything would have happened of itself; but as it is, it's out of the question — completely out of the question!"
Darya Alexandrovna sent him a letter asking for a side-saddle for Kitty's use. "I'm told you have a side-saddle," she wrote. "I hope you'll bring it over yourself."

This was more than he could bear. How could a woman with any intelligence, any tact, put her sister in such a humiliating position? He wrote ten notes, tore them all up, and sent the saddle without any reply. To write that he would come was impossible, because he could not come; to write that he could not come because something prevented him, or that he would be away, was worse. He sent the saddle without an answer, with a sense of having done something shameful. He handed over the now-revolting business of the estate to the bailiff and set off the next day to a remote district to see his friend Sviazhsky, who had splendid grouse marshes nearby and had recently written to remind him of a long-standing promise to stay with him. The grouse-marsh in the Surovsky district had long tempted Levin, but he had kept putting the trip off because of his work on the estate. Now he was glad to get away from the Shtcherbatskys' neighborhood, and even more from his farm work — especially on a shooting expedition, which in times of trouble had always been the best consolation.

chapters.title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: In the Surovsky district there was no railway and no post-horse service, so Levin drove there with his own horses in his big, old-fashioned carriage.

He stopped halfway at a well-off peasant's to feed his horses. A bald, well-preserved old man with a broad red beard going gray on his cheeks opened the gate, squeezing against the gatepost to let the three horses pass. He directed the coachman to a place under the shed in the big, clean, tidy yard with its charred, old-fashioned plows, and asked Levin to come into the parlor. A neatly dressed young woman, with clogs on her bare feet, was scrubbing the floor of the new outer room. She was startled by the dog, who ran in after Levin, and gave a shriek, but burst out laughing at her own fright as soon as she was told the dog wouldn't hurt her. Pointing the way to the parlor door with her bare arm, she bent down again, hiding her handsome face, and went on scrubbing.
"Would you like the samovar?" she asked.
"Yes, please."

The parlor was a big room with a Dutch stove and a screen dividing it in two. Under the holy pictures stood a table painted in patterns, a bench, and two chairs. Near the entrance was a dresser full of crockery. The shutters were closed, there were few flies, and the room was so clean that Levin worried Laska — who had been running along the road and bathing in puddles — would dirty the floor, and ordered her to a corner near the door. After looking around the parlor, Levin went out into the back yard. The good-looking young woman in clogs, swinging the empty pails on her yoke, ran ahead of him to the well for water.

"Look sharp, my girl!" the old man called after her good-humoredly, and he came over to Levin. "So, sir, are you on your way to Nikolay Ivanovitch Sviazhsky? His honor stops by here too," he began, leaning his elbows on the steps' railing and settling in for a chat. In the middle of the old man's account of his acquaintance with Sviazhsky, the gates creaked again, and laborers came into the yard from the fields with wooden plows and harrows. The horses harnessed to them were sleek and fat. The laborers were plainly of the household: two were young men in cotton shirts and caps, and the other two were hired laborers in homespun shirts — one an old man, the other a young fellow. Moving off from the steps, the old man went over to the horses and began unharnessing them.
"What have they been plowing?" Levin asked.
"Plowing up the potatoes. We rent a bit of land too. Fedot, don't let out the gelding — take him to the trough; we'll put the other one in harness."
"Father, the plowshares I ordered — has he brought them?" asked the big, healthy-looking fellow, plainly the old man's son.
"There — in the outer room," the old man answered, gathering up the harness he had taken off and flinging it on the ground. "You can fit them on while they have dinner."

The good-looking young woman came into the outer room with the full pails tugging at her shoulders. More women appeared from somewhere — young and handsome, middle-aged, old and ugly, with children and without.
The samovar began to sing; the laborers and the family, finished with the horses, came in for dinner. Levin got his provisions out of his carriage and invited the old man to take tea with him.
"Well, I've had some today already," said the old man, plainly accepting with pleasure. "But just a glass for company."

Over tea Levin heard all about the old man's farming. Ten years before, the old man had rented three hundred acres from the lady who owned them, and a year ago he had bought them outright and rented another three hundred from a neighboring landowner. A small part — the worst part — he let out for rent, while a hundred acres of arable land he cultivated himself with his family and two hired laborers. The old man complained that things were going badly. But Levin could see he was complaining out of a sense of decorum, and that his farm was in flourishing shape. If it hadn't been, he wouldn't have bought land at thirty-five roubles the acre, wouldn't have married off three sons and a nephew, wouldn't have rebuilt twice after fires — and each time on a larger scale. In spite of the complaints, it was plain that he was proud, and justly proud, of his prosperity, proud of his sons, his nephew, his sons' wives, his horses and cows, and most of all proud of holding the whole operation together. From his conversation with the old man, Levin thought he was not averse to new methods either. He had planted a great many potatoes, and his potatoes — as Levin had seen driving past — were already past flowering and starting to die down, while Levin's were only just coming into flower. He earthed up his potatoes with a modern plow borrowed from a neighboring landowner. He sowed wheat. The small fact that, when thinning his rye, the old man used the rye he thinned out as horse feed especially struck Levin. How many times Levin had seen this splendid fodder wasted and tried to get it saved; but it had always turned out to be impossible. The peasant got it done and couldn't praise it enough as feed for the beasts.
"What have the wenches to do? They carry it out in bundles to the roadside, and the cart brings it away."
"Well, we landowners can't manage well with our laborers," said Levin, passing him a glass of tea.

"Thank you," said the old man, taking the glass but refusing sugar, pointing at a lump he still had. "They're sheer ruin," he said. "Look at Sviazhsky's, for instance. We know what the land's like — first-rate — and yet there's not much of a crop to brag about. It isn't looked after — that's all it comes to!"
"But you work your land with hired laborers?"
"We're all peasants together. We go into everything ourselves. If a man's no use, he can go, and we'll manage on our own."
"Father, Finogen wants some tar," said the young woman in the clogs, coming in.
"Yes, yes, that's how it is, sir!" the old man said, getting up; and crossing himself deliberately, he thanked Levin and went out.

When Levin went into the kitchen to call his coachman, he saw the whole family at dinner. The women were standing up waiting on them. The young, sturdy-looking son was telling some funny story with his mouth full of pudding, and they were all laughing — the woman in the clogs, ladling cabbage soup into a bowl, laughing the most merrily of all.

Very likely the good-looking face of the young woman in clogs had a great deal to do with the sense of well-being this peasant household gave Levin, but the impression was so strong that Levin couldn't shake it off. All the way from the old peasant's to Sviazhsky's he kept turning back to this peasant farm, as though there were something in the impression that demanded special attention from him.

chapters.title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: Sviazhsky was the marshal of his district. He was five years older than Levin, and had been married a long while. His sister-in-law, a young woman Levin liked very much, lived with them, and Levin knew Sviazhsky and his wife would have been delighted to see her married off to him. He knew it with the certainty that so-called eligible young men always know such things, even if he could never have brought himself to mention it to anyone; and he knew too that, although he wanted to marry, and although by every measure this very attractive girl would make an excellent wife, he could no more have married her, even setting aside his love for Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, than he could have flown to the moon. And that knowledge poisoned the pleasure he had hoped to find in the visit.

When Sviazhsky's letter arrived with the shooting invitation, Levin had thought of all this at once; but even so he had decided that Sviazhsky's matchmaking ambitions for him were only his own groundless guess, and that he would go anyway. And, at the bottom of his heart, he wanted to test himself in regard to this girl. The Sviazhskys' home life was exceptionally pleasant, and Sviazhsky himself, the best example Levin knew of a man involved in local public affairs, was very interesting to him.

Sviazhsky was one of those people who never stopped puzzling Levin — people whose convictions, perfectly logical though never original, run along one track on their own, while their actual life, very definite and firm in its direction, runs along another track entirely and almost always in direct contradiction. Sviazhsky was an extremely progressive man. He looked down on the nobility, believed that most of his fellow nobles secretly favored serfdom and were only hiding it out of cowardice, and regarded Russia as a ruined country, somewhere along the lines of Turkey, with a government so bad he never permitted himself to criticize its actions seriously — and yet he was a functionary of that government, a model marshal of the nobility, and whenever he drove out he wore the official cockade and the cap with the red band. He considered human life only tolerable abroad, and he went abroad at every chance — while at the same time running an elaborate, improved farming operation in Russia and following with the keenest interest everything happening in the country. He believed the Russian peasant occupied an evolutionary stage somewhere between ape and man, and yet in the local assemblies no one was quicker to shake hands with peasants and listen to their views. He believed neither in God nor the devil, but he worried a great deal about improving the clergy and maintaining their income, and he made a special effort to keep the village church in good repair.

On the woman question he was firmly with the radicals — full liberty for women, especially the right to work. And yet he and his wife lived together on such terms that their affectionate, childless household was the envy of everyone, and he arranged his wife's days so that she did nothing, and could do nothing, except share in his efforts to fill her time as happily and agreeably as possible.

If it hadn't been part of Levin's nature to put the kindest interpretation on people, Sviazhsky's character would have presented no puzzle at all: he would simply have said to himself, "a fool or a knave," and everything would have been clear. But he couldn't say "fool," because Sviazhsky was unmistakably intelligent — and, more than that, a highly cultivated man who was unusually modest about his culture. There was no subject he knew nothing about. But he didn't put his knowledge on display unless he had to. Still less could Levin call him a knave, since he was plainly an honest, kindhearted, sensible man who went about his work with good humor, sharp focus, and persistence; he was held in high regard by everyone around him, and he had certainly never knowingly done — and was indeed incapable of doing — anything base.
Levin tried to make sense of him and couldn't, and so he looked at him and his life as at a living enigma.

He and Sviazhsky were on friendly terms, and so Levin used to test him, trying to get down to the very foundation of his view of life; but it was always useless. Every time Levin tried to push past the outer chambers of Sviazhsky's mind — chambers hospitably open to anyone — he saw Sviazhsky grow faintly uncomfortable; a flicker of alarm would show in his eyes, as though he were afraid Levin would understand him, and he would give Levin a kindly, good-natured rebuff.

Just now, in his disillusionment with farming, Levin was especially glad to stay with Sviazhsky. Apart from the fact that the sight of this happy, affectionate couple, so satisfied with themselves and with everyone else, and their well-run household, always lifted his spirits, he felt a longing — now that he was so dissatisfied with his own life — to get at whatever secret Sviazhsky had that gave him such clarity, definiteness, and good courage in living. Beyond that, Levin knew that at Sviazhsky's he would meet the local landowners, and right now he was particularly eager to hear and join in those country conversations about crops, wages, and the rest — talk that, he was aware, is conventionally dismissed as something very low, but which seemed to him at the moment to be the one subject that mattered. "Maybe it wasn't important in the days of serfdom, and maybe it isn't important in England. In both cases the conditions of agriculture have been firmly settled; but with us, now that everything has been turned upside down and is only just beginning to take shape, the question of what form these conditions will take is the only question that matters in Russia," Levin thought.

The shooting turned out worse than Levin had expected. The marsh was dry and there were no grouse to speak of. He walked all day and came back with only three birds, but he brought back, as he always did from a day in the field, an excellent appetite, excellent spirits, and the kind of sharp, intellectual mood that with him always followed hard physical exertion. And out in the marsh, when he seemed to be thinking of nothing in particular, the old peasant and his family kept coming back to him, and the impression they had left seemed to demand not just his attention but the resolution of some question tied up with them.
In the evening, at tea, two landowners had come on some business about a wardship and joined the party, and the kind of conversation Levin had been hoping for started up.

Levin was sitting beside his hostess at the tea table, and he had to keep up some sort of conversation with her and with her sister, who was across from him. Madame Sviazhskaya was a round-faced, fair-haired, rather short woman, all smiles and dimples. Levin tried to use her to get at the formidable puzzle her husband presented to him; but his thoughts weren't entirely free, because he was in agonies of embarrassment. The cause was the sister-in-law, sitting directly across from him in a dress — put on, he imagined, specifically for his benefit — cut particularly low, trapeze-shaped, over her white bosom. That quadrangular opening, despite the bosom being very white — or precisely because it was so very white — robbed Levin of the full use of his wits. He imagined, probably wrongly, that the low-cut bodice had been made on his account, and he felt he had no right to look at it, and tried not to look at it; but he also felt that he was somehow to blame for its having been made in the first place. It seemed to him that he had deceived someone, that he owed someone an explanation, that no such explanation was possible — and for that reason he kept blushing, fidgeting, and saying the wrong thing. His awkwardness rubbed off on the pretty sister-in-law too. But their hostess seemed not to notice, and kept deliberately drawing her into the conversation.

"You say," she was saying, picking up the subject they had started on, "that my husband can't be interested in anything Russian. On the contrary — he's always in cheerful spirits abroad, but not the way he is here. Here he feels in his proper place. He has so much to do, and he has a knack for taking an interest in everything. Oh — you haven't been to see our school, have you?"
"I have seen it... The little house covered in ivy, isn't it?"
"Yes; that's Nastia's work," she said, nodding toward her sister.
"Do you teach there yourself?" Levin asked, trying to look above the low neckline but feeling that wherever he looked in that direction he would see it.
"Yes; I used to teach there myself, and I still do, but we have a first-rate schoolmistress now. And we've added gymnastic exercises."

"No, thank you, no more tea for me," Levin said, and, knowing he was being rude but unable to keep up the conversation, he stood up, blushing. "I hear an interesting conversation," he added, and walked off to the other end of the table, where Sviazhsky was sitting with the two country gentlemen. Sviazhsky was sitting sideways, one elbow on the table, a cup in one hand, while with the other he was gathering up his beard, holding it to his nose, then letting it fall again, as though he were smelling it. His brilliant black eyes were fixed on the excited country gentleman with gray whiskers, and he was apparently enjoying the man's remarks. The gentleman was complaining about the peasants. It was clear to Levin that Sviazhsky had a ready answer that would have demolished the man's whole position, but that he couldn't deliver it from where he stood, and was instead listening, not without pleasure, to the landowner's comic tirade.

The gentleman with the gray whiskers was plainly an unrepentant defender of serfdom and a devoted farmer who had spent his whole life in the country. Levin saw the proof in his clothes — the old-fashioned, threadbare coat that was obviously not his everyday wear — in his shrewd, deep-set eyes, in his idiomatic, fluent Russian, in the commanding tone that long use had made habitual, and in the firm gestures of his large, red, sun-darkened hands, with an old betrothal ring on the little finger.

chapters.title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: "If I'd only the heart to give up what's been set in motion... so much trouble wasted... I'd turn my back on the whole thing, sell up, go off like Nikolay Ivanovitch... to hear _La Belle Hélène_," said the landowner, a pleasant smile lighting up his shrewd old face.
"But you don't give it up," said Nikolay Ivanovitch Sviazhsky; "so there must be something in it for you."

"The only thing in it for me is that I live in my own house — neither bought nor rented. Beyond that, one keeps hoping the people will come to their senses. Though it's the other way round — you wouldn't believe the drunkenness, the immorality! They keep cutting up their bits of land and swapping them around. Not a sight of a horse or a cow anywhere. The peasant is dying of hunger, but just try taking him on as a hired hand — he'll do his best to spite you, and then haul you up before the justice of the peace."
"But you go to the justice yourself," Sviazhsky said.

"Lodge complaints? Not for anything in the world! Such talk and such a fuss — you'd be sorry you ever started. Take the works — they pocketed the advance and ran off. What did the justice do? Acquitted them. Nothing keeps them in line but their own village court and their village elder. He'll flog them the old-fashioned way! Take that away and there's nothing left but to throw it all up and run."
Plainly the landowner was teasing Sviazhsky, who, far from taking offense, seemed to be enjoying it.
"But we run our places without anything that extreme," he said, smiling. "Levin and I — and this gentleman."
He indicated the other landowner.
"Yes, the thing's being done at Mihail Petrovitch's — but ask him how. Do you call that a rational system?" said the landowner, obviously rather pleased with the word "rational."

"My system is very simple," said Mihail Petrovitch. "Thank God. My whole management comes down to having the money ready for the autumn taxes, and the peasants come to me — 'Father, master, help us!' Well, they're all one's neighbors; one feels for them. So one fronts them a third, but one says, 'Remember, lads — I have helped you, and you must help me when I need it — whether it's the sowing of the oats, or the haymaking, or the harvest'; and they agree, so much for each taxpayer — though some of them are dishonest, that's true."
Levin, who had long been familiar with these patriarchal arrangements, exchanged a look with Sviazhsky and cut Mihail Petrovitch off, turning back to the gentleman with the gray whiskers.
"Then what do you think?" he asked. "What sort of system should one go with nowadays?"

"Manage the way Mihail Petrovitch does — or rent the land out for half the crop or for cash to the peasants. You can do that — only that's exactly how the general prosperity of the country is being destroyed. Where the land used to yield nine to one with serf labor and proper management, on the half-crop system it yields three to one. Russia has been ruined by the emancipation!"

Sviazhsky looked at Levin with smiling eyes and even made a small ironic gesture at him; but Levin didn't find the landowner's words ridiculous — he understood them better than he understood Sviazhsky. A good deal more of what the gentleman with the gray whiskers said in support of his view that Russia had been ruined by the emancipation struck Levin as quite true, new to him, and impossible to argue against. The landowner was plainly voicing his own thought — something that happens very rarely — and a thought he hadn't arrived at out of a need to exercise an idle mind, but one that had grown up out of the conditions of his life, that he had brooded over in the solitude of his village and considered from every angle.

"The point, you see, is that progress of any kind only happens through the exercise of authority," he said, plainly wanting to show that he was not without culture. "Take the reforms of Peter, of Catherine, of Alexander. Take European history. And progress in agriculture more than anywhere else — the potato, for instance, was introduced among us by force. The wooden plough wasn't always used either. It was probably brought in sometime before the Empire, but it was brought in by force. Now, in our own time, we landowners under serfdom introduced all sorts of improvements: drying machines, threshing machines, the cartage of manure, all the modern implements — we brought all of it in on our own authority, and the peasants opposed it at first, and then ended up imitating us. Now, with the abolition of serfdom, our authority has been taken away; and so our farming, where it had been raised to a high level, is bound to sink back to the most primitive, savage condition. That's how I see it."
"But why? If it's rational, you'll be able to maintain the same system with hired labor," Sviazhsky said.
"We have no power over them. With whom, may I ask, am I going to run the system?"
"There it is — the labor force — the central element of agriculture," Levin thought.
"With laborers."

"The laborers won't work properly, and won't work with good implements. Our laborer can do nothing but get drunk like a pig, and once he's drunk he ruins whatever you give him. He makes the horses sick on too much water, he cuts good harness, he barters the wheel tires for drink, he drops bits of iron into the threshing machine just to break it. He hates the sight of anything that isn't done in his usual way. And that's how the level of farming has dropped everywhere. Lands gone out of cultivation, overgrown with weeds, or carved up among the peasants, and where millions of bushels used to be raised you get a hundred thousand; the wealth of the country has gone down. If the same thing had been done, but with proper care..."
And he went on to lay out his own scheme of emancipation, which, in his view, would have avoided all these drawbacks.
This didn't interest Levin, but when the landowner was done, Levin went back to his earlier point and, turning to Sviazhsky, tried to draw out a serious opinion from him.

"That the standard of farming is dropping, and that under our current relationship to the peasants there is no possibility of running an operation on a rational system that turns a profit — that's perfectly true," he said.

"I don't believe it," Sviazhsky answered, quite seriously. "All I see is that we don't know how to cultivate the land, and that our farming under serfdom was not too advanced, but actually too primitive. We have no machinery, no good stock, no proper supervision; we don't even know how to keep accounts. Ask any landowner — he can't tell you which crop is profitable and which isn't."
"Italian bookkeeping," said the gentleman with the gray whiskers ironically. "You can keep your books however you like, but if they ruin everything for you, there'll be no profit anyway."

"Why do they ruin things? They'll break a poor threshing machine, or your Russian press — but they don't break my steam press. They'll ruin a wretched Russian nag — but give them good dray horses and the dray horses are fine. It's the same all the way around. We have to lift our farming to a higher level."
"Oh, if only one had the means, Nikolay Ivanovitch! It's easy enough for you; but for me, with a son at the university and boys at the high school — how am I going to buy dray horses?"
"That's what the land banks are for."
"So that what I have left can be auctioned off? No, thank you."

"I don't agree that it's necessary or even possible to raise the level of agriculture any further," Levin said. "I throw myself into it, I have means, and I can do nothing. As for the banks — I don't know who they actually help. For my part, anyway, whatever I've spent money on in the way of farming, it's been a loss: livestock — a loss, machinery — a loss."
"That's true enough," the gentleman with the gray whiskers chimed in, positively laughing with satisfaction.

"And I'm not the only one," Levin went on. "I see all the neighboring landowners who are working their land on a rational system; almost without exception they're doing it at a loss. Come, tell us — does your land pay?" Levin asked, and at once he caught in Sviazhsky's eyes that fleeting expression of alarm he had noticed every time he tried to push past the outer chambers of Sviazhsky's mind.
