Levin said to Veslovsky, staring fixedly at his leg but speaking with that forced friendliness Kitty knew so well in him, and which was so unlike him. "I can't promise grouse, but there are plenty of snipe. Only we'll need to start early. You're not tired? Stiva, you're not tired?"
"Me, tired? I've never been tired in my life. We could stay up all night, for all I care. Let's go for a walk!"
"Yes, really, let's not go to bed at all! Wonderful!" Veslovsky chimed in.

"Oh, we all know you can go without sleep and keep other people up too," Dolly said to her husband, with that faint trace of irony that had become almost permanent in her voice when she spoke to him. "But as far as I'm concerned, it's time for bed... I'm going up, I don't want any supper."
"No, stay a little longer, Dolly," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, coming round to her side of the supper table. "I still have so much to tell you."
"Nothing important, I'm sure."
"Did you know Veslovsky has been to Anna's, and he's going back? They're hardly fifty miles from you, you know, and I really must go over there too. Veslovsky, come over here!"
Vassenka crossed over to the ladies and sat down beside Kitty.
"Tell me, please — you stayed with her? How was she?" Darya Alexandrovna asked him.

Levin was left at the other end of the table, and although he kept up his conversation with the princess and Varenka without a pause, he could see that something eager and mysterious was being discussed between Stepan Arkadyevitch, Dolly, Kitty, and Veslovsky. And that wasn't all. He saw on his wife's face a look of real feeling as she gazed, eyes fixed, at Vassenka's handsome face while he told them something with great animation.
"It's an exceptionally nice place," Veslovsky was saying about Vronsky and Anna. "I can't presume to judge, of course, but in their house you really do feel the sense of a home."
"What are they planning to do?"
"I believe they're thinking of going to Moscow."
"How splendid it would be if we all went over together! When are you going?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked Vassenka.
"I'm spending July there."
"Will you go?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said to his wife.

"I've been wanting to for a long time, and I certainly will," said Dolly. "I feel sorry for her, and I know her. She's a splendid woman. I'll go alone, when you've gone back, and then I won't be in anyone's way. It will actually be better without you."
"Of course," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "And you, Kitty?"
"Me? Why would I go?" Kitty said, flushing scarlet, and glanced over at her husband.
"Do you know Anna Arkadyevna, then?" Veslovsky asked her. "She's a very fascinating woman."
"Yes," she answered Veslovsky, blushing even deeper. She got up and walked over to her husband.
"So you're going shooting tomorrow?" she said.

His jealousy, in those few minutes — especially at the flush that had spread across her cheeks while she was talking to Veslovsky — had already gone a long way. Now, as he heard her words, he gave them his own twist. Strange as it seemed to him later when he looked back on it, in that instant it appeared perfectly clear to him that in asking whether he was going shooting all she really wanted to know was whether he would be giving that pleasure to Vassenka Veslovsky, with whom, he imagined, she was in love.
"Yes, I'm going," he answered her in an unnatural voice that he himself found unpleasant.
"No, better stay home tomorrow, otherwise Dolly will hardly see her husband at all, and set off the day after," said Kitty.
The motive behind Kitty's words was translated by Levin like this: "Don't separate me from _him_. I don't mind _your_ going, but do let me enjoy the company of this delightful young man."
"Oh, if you'd like, we'll stay home tomorrow," Levin answered, with peculiar friendliness.
Meanwhile Vassenka, with no idea of the misery his presence was causing, got up from the table after Kitty, and, watching her with smiling, admiring eyes, followed after her.
Levin caught that look. He went white, and for a moment he could hardly draw a breath. "How dare he look at my wife that way!" was the feeling boiling inside him.
"Tomorrow, then? Please, let's go," said Vassenka, sitting down on a chair and crossing his leg in his usual way again.

Levin's jealousy ran further still. He could already see himself as a deceived husband whom his wife and her lover regarded as nothing more than a convenient supplier of comforts and amusements... But in spite of all that, he politely and hospitably questioned Vassenka about his shooting, his gun, and his boots, and agreed to go out the next day.

Luckily for Levin, the old princess cut short his torment by standing up herself and advising Kitty to go to bed. But even now Levin could not escape another stab. As he was saying good night to his hostess, Vassenka tried once more to kiss her hand, but Kitty, reddening, pulled her hand back and said, with a naive bluntness for which the old princess scolded her afterwards:
"That isn't the way we do things."
In Levin's eyes she was at fault for having allowed such manners to take hold in the first place, and even more at fault for showing so clumsily that she didn't like them.

"How can anyone want to go to bed!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who, after several glasses of wine at supper, was now in his most charming and sentimental mood. "Look, Kitty," he said, pointing to the moon, which had just risen behind the lime trees, "isn't it exquisite! Veslovsky, this is the time for a serenade. You know, he has a wonderful voice — we practiced songs together along the road. He's brought some lovely songs with him, two new ones. Varvara Andreevna and he must sing some duets."
When the party had broken up, Stepan Arkadyevitch walked for a long while along the avenue with Veslovsky; their voices could be heard singing one of the new songs.

Listening to those voices, Levin sat scowling in an armchair in his wife's bedroom and kept up an obstinate silence when she asked him what was wrong. But when at last, with a timid glance, she ventured the question — "Was there perhaps something about Veslovsky you didn't like?" — it all burst out, and he told her everything. He was humiliated by what he was saying, and that infuriated him all the more.

He stood facing her, his eyes glittering menacingly under his drawn brows, his strong arms pressed across his chest as if he were straining every nerve to keep himself in check. The expression on his face would have been grim, even cruel, if it had not at the same time carried a look of suffering that touched her. His jaws were twitching, and his voice kept breaking.

"You have to understand that I am not jealous — jealousy is an ugly word. I can't be jealous, believe me... I can't say what I feel, but this is awful... I'm not jealous, but I am wounded, humiliated that anyone should dare think — that anyone should dare look at you with eyes like that."
"Eyes like what?" Kitty said, trying as scrupulously as she could to recall every word and gesture of that evening, and every nuance behind them.

At the very bottom of her heart she did think there had been something — precisely at the moment when he had crossed over after her to the other end of the table; but she didn't dare admit it even to herself, much less bring herself to say so to him and so increase his suffering.
"And what could possibly be attractive about me in the state I'm in now?..."
"Ah!" he cried, clutching his head, "you mustn't say that!... If you had been attractive then..."

"Oh no, Kostya, oh, wait — listen!" she said, looking at him with an expression of pained pity. "What can you be thinking? When for me there's no one else in the world, no one, no one!... Would you like me never to see anyone?"

For the first instant she had been offended by his jealousy; she had been angry that even the slightest amusement, even the most innocent one, should be forbidden her. But now she would gladly have sacrificed not only such trifles but everything else for his peace of mind, to spare him the agony he was going through.

"You have to understand the horror and the absurdity of my position," he went on in a desperate whisper. "That he's in my house, that strictly speaking he hasn't done anything improper apart from his free-and-easy manner and the way he sits with his legs tucked up. He thinks it's the height of style, so I'm forced to be civil to him."
"But Kostya, you're exaggerating," said Kitty, secretly rejoicing at the depth of his love for her, which was showing itself now in his jealousy.

"The most awful part of it all is that you are just as you've always been, and now especially, when for me you are something sacred, and we are so happy, so particularly happy — and all of a sudden a little wretch... He's not a little wretch; why am I abusing him? I have nothing to do with him. But why should my happiness, and yours..."
"Do you know, I understand now where it all came from," Kitty was beginning.
"Well, what? what?"
"I saw the way you looked at us while we were talking at supper."
"Well, well!" Levin said in dismay.

She told him what they had been talking about. As she told him, she was breathless with feeling. Levin was silent for a moment, then scanned her pale, distressed face, and suddenly clutched at his head.
"Katya, I've been tormenting you! Darling, forgive me! It's madness! Katya, I'm a criminal. And how could you be so upset over such an idiotic thing?"
"Oh, I was just sorry for you."
"For me? for me? How insane I am!... But why make you miserable? It's awful to think that any outsider can shatter our happiness."
"It's humiliating too, of course."
"Well then, I'll keep him here all summer and drown him in courtesy," said Levin, kissing her hands. "You'll see. Tomorrow... Oh yes, we're going tomorrow."

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The next day, before the ladies were up, the wagonette and a trap for the shooting party were already at the door, and Laska, who had known since early morning that they were going shooting, had whined and darted back and forth and then settled herself in the wagonette beside the coachman, where, disapproving of the delay, she watched the door intently for the sportsmen who still did not appear. The first to come out was Vassenka Veslovsky, in new high boots that reached halfway up his thick thighs, in a green blouse, with a new Russian-leather cartridge belt, and his Scottish cap with ribbons, carrying a brand-new English gun without a sling. Laska flew up to him, welcomed him, jumped up and asked him in her own way whether the others were coming soon, and when she got no answer she returned to her post and sank back into stillness, head tilted, one ear pricked to listen. At last the door opened with a creak, and Stepan Arkadyevitch's spotted-and-tan pointer Krak flew out, running in circles and turning over in the air. Stepan Arkadyevitch himself followed, gun in hand and cigar in his mouth.

"Good dog, good dog, Krak!" he called encouragingly to the dog, who had put his paws up on his chest and was snapping at his game bag. Stepan Arkadyevitch was got up in rough leggings and spats, torn trousers, and a short coat. On his head was the wreck of a hat of no particular shape, but his gun, of a new patent, was a perfect gem, and his game bag and cartridge belt, though worn, were of the very best quality.

Until now, Vassenka Veslovsky had had no idea that it was truly _chic_ for a sportsman to dress in rags while keeping his shooting equipment of the finest quality. He saw it now, looking at Stepan Arkadyevitch — radiant in his tatters, graceful, well-fed, and cheerful, the picture of a Russian gentleman. And he made up his mind that next time he went shooting he would definitely adopt the same look.
"Well, and what about our host?" he asked.
"A young wife," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Yes — and such a charming one!"
"He came down already dressed. No doubt he's gone back up to her again."

Stepan Arkadyevitch had guessed correctly. Levin had run upstairs again to ask his wife one more time whether she forgave him for his idiocy the night before, and also to beg her, for Christ's sake, to be more careful. The main thing was that she keep clear of the children — they could bump into her at any moment. Then he had to hear her say once more that she was not angry with him for going away for two days, and to plead with her to send him a note by a servant on horseback the next morning, to write him even just two words, to let him know that everything was all right with her.

Kitty was upset, as she always was when she had to part with her husband for a couple of days, but when she saw his eager figure, looking big and strong in his shooting boots and white blouse, and saw a kind of hunter's elation and excitement she could not begin to share, she forgot her own dejection for the sake of his pleasure and said goodbye to him cheerfully.
"Pardon, gentlemen!" he said, running out onto the steps. "Did you put in the lunch? Why is the chestnut on the right? Well, never mind. Laska, down — go and lie down!"
"Put it in with the herd of oxen," he said to the herdsman who had been waiting for him at the steps with some question. "Excuse me, here comes another nuisance."
Levin jumped down from the wagonette, where he had already taken his seat, to meet the carpenter, who was coming toward the steps with a ruler in his hand.
"You didn't come to the office yesterday, and now you're holding me up. Well, what is it?"
"Would your honor let me put in another turn? It's only three steps to add. And we'd make it fit just right at the same time. It would be a lot more convenient."
"You should have listened to me," Levin answered with annoyance. "I said to mark the lines first and then fit the steps. Now there's no putting it right. Do as I told you, and build a new staircase."

The trouble was that in the lodge being built the carpenter had ruined the staircase by assembling it without calculating the space it had to fill, so that once it was put in place all the steps came out sloping. Now the carpenter wanted to keep the same staircase and add three more steps.
"It will work much better."
"But where is your staircase going to come out, with its three extra steps?"

"Why, upon my word, sir," the carpenter said with a contemptuous smile. "It comes out right at the right spot. It starts, so to speak," he said with a persuasive gesture, "and it comes down and comes down, and it comes out."
"But three more steps will add to the length, too... where is it going to come out?"
"Why, sure enough, it'll start from the bottom and go up and go up, and come out like so," the carpenter said, stubborn and convinced.
"It'll hit the ceiling and the wall."
"Upon my word! It'll go up and up and come out like this."
Levin took out a ramrod and started sketching the staircase for him in the dust.
"There, do you see?"
"Whatever your honor says," the carpenter said, with a sudden flash in his eyes that showed he had finally understood. "Looks like it'll be best to build a new one."
"Well, then, do as you're told," Levin shouted, settling himself in the wagonette. "Down! Hold the dogs, Philip!"

With all his family and household worries left behind, Levin now felt such a keen sense of joy and anticipation that he was in no mood to talk. On top of that, he had that concentrated excitement every sportsman feels as he approaches the field. If anything was on his mind at the moment, it was only the question of whether they would find anything in the Kolpensky marsh, whether Laska would show to advantage next to Krak, and whether he would shoot well that day himself. Not to disgrace himself in front of a newcomer — not to be outdone by Oblonsky — that, too, crossed his mind.

Oblonsky was feeling the same and was also not talkative. Vassenka Veslovsky alone kept up a steady flow of cheerful chatter. As he listened to him now, Levin felt ashamed of how unfair he had been to him the day before. Vassenka really was a nice fellow — simple, kind-hearted, and good-humored. If Levin had met him before he was married, he would have made friends with him. Levin did rather dislike his holiday attitude to life and a certain easy assumption of elegance — as if he took it for granted that he was a person of unquestionable importance because he had long nails, a stylish cap, and so on to match. But that could be forgiven on account of his good nature and good breeding. Levin liked him for his good education, for the fact that he spoke French and English with such an excellent accent, and for being a man of his own world.

Vassenka was thoroughly delighted with the left-hand horse, which came from the Don steppes. He kept praising it enthusiastically. "How fine it must be to gallop over the steppes on a steppe horse! Don't you think?" he said. He had imagined riding a steppe horse as something wild and romantic, and it had turned out to be nothing of the kind. But his simplicity, especially combined with his good looks, his pleasant smile, and the grace of his movements, was very attractive. Whether because Vassenka's nature was congenial to him, or because Levin was trying to make up for his sins of the night before by seeing only what was good in him, he genuinely enjoyed his company.

After they had driven a couple of miles from home, Veslovsky suddenly reached for a cigar and his wallet, and could not tell whether he had lost them or left them on the table. In the wallet there were thirty-seven pounds, and so the matter could not simply be left in doubt.
"Tell you what, Levin, I'll gallop home on that left trace horse. That would be splendid. Eh?" he said, getting ready to climb down.
"No, why should you?" Levin answered, calculating that Vassenka could hardly weigh less than seventeen stone. "I'll send the coachman."
The coachman rode back on the trace horse, and Levin himself drove the remaining pair.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: "Well, then, what's the plan of campaign? Tell us everything," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.

"Here's the plan. Right now we're driving to Gvozdyov. At Gvozdyov, on this side, there's a grouse marsh, and on the other side of the village there are some magnificent snipe marshes, where there are also grouse. It's hot now, and we'll get there toward evening — it's about fifteen miles — and do some evening shooting; we'll spend the night there and go on tomorrow to the bigger moors."
"And there's nothing on the way?"
"Yes, but we ought to save ourselves; besides, it's hot. There are two nice little spots, but I doubt there'll be anything to shoot."

Levin would have liked to stop at those little spots himself, but they were close to home; he could shoot them any time, and they were only little places — there would barely be room for three guns. So, with a bit of dishonesty, he said he doubted there would be anything to shoot. When they reached a small marsh, Levin would have driven straight past, but Stepan Arkadyevitch, with the practiced eye of a sportsman, immediately spotted the reeds from the road.
"Shall we give it a try?" he said, pointing at the little marsh.
"Levin, please! How splendid!" Vassenka Veslovsky began begging, and Levin could only give in.
Before they even had time to stop, the dogs had flown one after the other into the marsh.
"Krak! Laska!..."
The dogs came back.

"There won't be room for three of us. I'll stay here," Levin said, hoping they would find nothing but the peewits that the dogs had startled and that were now turning in flight, wailing plaintively over the marsh.
"No! Come on, Levin, let's go together!" Veslovsky called.
"Really, there's no room. Laska, back, Laska! You don't need another dog, do you?"

Levin stayed behind with the wagonette and watched the sportsmen enviously. They walked clear across the marsh. Apart from little birds and peewits, of which Vassenka shot one, there was nothing in the marsh.
"You see now I wasn't being stingy about the marsh," Levin said, "it was just a waste of time."

"Oh no, it was great fun all the same. Did you see me?" said Vassenka Veslovsky, clambering awkwardly into the wagonette with his gun and his peewit in his hands. "How splendidly I shot that bird! Didn't I? Well, will we soon be at the real spot?"

The horses suddenly jolted forward, Levin knocked his head against the stock of someone's gun, and there was the crack of a shot. Actually the gun went off first, but to Levin it seemed the other way around. It turned out that Vassenka Veslovsky had only pulled one trigger and left the other hammer cocked. The charge flew into the ground without doing any harm. Stepan Arkadyevitch shook his head and laughed reprovingly at Veslovsky, but Levin couldn't bring himself to scold him. For one thing, any rebuke would have looked like a reaction to the danger and the bump now rising on Levin's forehead. And besides, Veslovsky was at first so naively distressed, and then laughed so good-humoredly and infectiously at the general consternation, that you couldn't help laughing with him.

When they reached the second marsh, which was fairly large and would take some time to shoot through, Levin tried to talk them out of stopping. But once again Veslovsky talked him into it. And again, since the marsh was narrow, Levin played the good host and stayed with the carriage.

Krak headed straight for some clumps of sedge. Vassenka Veslovsky was the first to run after the dog. Before Stepan Arkadyevitch had time to catch up, a grouse flew out. Veslovsky missed it, and it flew off into an unmown meadow. That grouse was now left for Veslovsky to follow up. Krak found it again and pointed, Veslovsky shot it, and then went back to the carriage. "Now you go and I'll stay with the horses," he said.
Levin had begun to feel the pangs of a sportsman's envy. He handed the reins to Veslovsky and walked into the marsh.
Laska, who had been whining piteously at the injustice of her treatment, shot straight ahead toward a promising spot Levin knew well, and that Krak had not yet covered.
"Why don't you call her back?" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted.
"She won't scare them," Levin answered, sharing his bitch's excitement and hurrying after her.

The closer Laska got to the familiar nesting places, the more focused her searching became. A little marsh bird distracted her for no more than an instant. She made one circuit of the clump of reeds, was starting a second, and suddenly quivered with excitement and froze.

"Come on, come on, Stiva!" Levin shouted, feeling his heart starting to pound; and suddenly, as though some shutter had been thrown open inside his straining ears, every sound — confused but loud — began to beat against his hearing, all sense of distance lost. He heard Stepan Arkadyevitch's footsteps and mistook them for the distant trampling of the horses; he heard the brittle snap of twigs underfoot and took it for a grouse taking off. He also heard, not far behind him, a splashing in the water that he could not explain to himself.
Picking his way carefully, he moved up to the dog.
"Fetch it!"

Not a grouse but a snipe flew up from beside the dog. Levin had raised his gun, but at the very moment he was taking aim the splashing grew louder, came closer, and merged with the sound of Veslovsky's voice shouting something with strange loudness. Levin saw that he was pointing his gun behind the snipe, but he fired anyway.
Once he was sure he had missed, Levin looked around and saw the horses and the wagonette not on the road but out in the marsh.
Veslovsky, eager to see the shooting, had driven the horses into the marsh, and they had gotten stuck in the mud.

"Damn the fellow!" Levin muttered to himself as he walked back to the carriage sunk in the mire. "What did you drive in there for?" he said dryly to him, and called the coachman over and started hauling the horses out.

Levin was annoyed at having had his shooting interrupted, annoyed at the horses being stuck in the mud, and even more annoyed at the fact that neither Stepan Arkadyevitch nor Veslovsky was helping him and the coachman to unharness the horses and get them out, since neither of them had the faintest idea about harnessing. Without bothering to answer a syllable of Vassenka's protest that the ground had been perfectly dry there, Levin worked in silence with the coachman to get the horses free. But then, as he warmed up to the work and saw how energetically Veslovsky was tugging at the wagonette by one of the mudguards — so hard that he actually broke it — Levin reproached himself for having let yesterday's feelings make him too cold toward Veslovsky, and he tried to be especially friendly to smooth over his earlier chill. Once everything was put right and the carriage was back on the road, Levin had the lunch served.

"_Bon appétit — bonne conscience! Ce poulet va tomber jusqu'au fond de mes bottes_," quoted Vassenka, his spirits restored, as he finished his second chicken. "Well, now our troubles are over, and everything will go beautifully. Only, to atone for my sins, I'm bound to ride on the box. Right? Eh? No, no! I'll be your Automedon. You'll see how I drive you," he replied, not letting go of the rein when Levin asked him to let the coachman drive. "No, I have to atone for my sins, and I'm very comfortable on the box." And so he drove.

Levin was a little worried that he would wear the horses out, especially the chestnut, which Veslovsky did not know how to hold in; but, without realizing it, he came under the spell of his cheerfulness and listened all the way to the songs Veslovsky sang on the box, and to his descriptions and imitations of driving English-style, four-in-hand. So it was in the very best of spirits that they drove on after lunch to the Gvozdyov marsh.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Vassenka drove the horses so briskly that they reached the marsh too early, while it was still hot.

As they approached this more important marsh — the main goal of their expedition — Levin couldn't help wondering how he might get rid of Vassenka and be free to move on his own. Stepan Arkadyevitch clearly had the same wish, and on his face Levin saw the look of anxiety always present in a true sportsman at the start of a shoot, together with a certain good-humored slyness that belonged to him alone.

"How shall we go about it? It's a splendid marsh, I see, and there are hawks," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, pointing at two large birds hovering over the reeds. "Where there are hawks, there's bound to be game."

"Now, gentlemen," said Levin, pulling up his boots and checking the lock of his gun with a rather gloomy expression, "do you see those reeds?" He pointed to an island of blackish green in the huge, half-mown wet meadow that stretched along the right bank of the river. "The marsh starts here, straight in front of us, you see — where it's greener? From here it runs off to the right, where the horses are; there are breeding places there, and grouse, and all around those reeds as far as that alder, and right up to the mill. Look, over there, where the pools are. That's the best spot. I once shot seventeen snipe there. We'll split up with the dogs and go in different directions, and then meet up at the mill."
"All right, who goes left and who goes right?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked. "It's wider to the right; the two of you take that side, and I'll take the left," he added, with apparent indifference.
"Capital! We'll bring back the bigger bag! Yes, come on, come on!" Vassenka exclaimed.
Levin could only agree, and they split up.

As soon as they entered the marsh, the two dogs began to hunt together, working toward the green, slime-covered pool. Levin knew Laska's method — wary and noncommittal; he knew the spot too, and was expecting a whole covey of snipe.

"Veslovsky, walk beside me, beside me!" he said in a low voice to his companion, who was splashing in the water behind him. After that stray shot near the Kolpensky marsh, Levin couldn't help being uneasy about which way Vassenka's gun was pointed.
"Oh, I won't get in your way — don't worry about me."

But Levin couldn't help worrying, and he remembered Kitty's parting words: "Mind you don't shoot each other." The dogs were drawing closer, then passing each other, each following its own scent. The expectation of snipe was so intense that to Levin the squelch of his own heel as he dragged it up out of the mire sounded like a snipe's call, and he gripped and tightened his hand on the lock of his gun.

"Bang! Bang!" sounded almost in his ear. Vassenka had fired at a flock of ducks that was floating over the marsh and flying toward the sportsmen at that moment, far out of range. Before Levin had time to look around, there was the whir of one snipe, then another, then a third, and some eight more rose one after another.

Stepan Arkadyevitch hit one just as it was starting its zigzag flight, and the snipe dropped in a heap into the mud. Oblonsky took deliberate aim at another, still flying low over the reeds, and at the same instant as his shot that snipe too came down, and it could be seen fluttering out where the sedge had been cut, its undamaged wing showing white underneath.

Levin was not so lucky: he fired too low at his first bird and missed; he aimed at it again, just as it was rising, but at that instant another snipe flew up right at his feet, distracting him, so that he missed again.

While they were reloading their guns, another snipe rose, and Veslovsky, who had managed to reload in time, sent two charges of small shot uselessly into the water. Stepan Arkadyevitch picked up his snipe, and with sparkling eyes glanced at Levin.
"Well, let's split up now," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, and limping on his left foot, holding his gun ready and whistling to his dog, he set off in one direction. Levin and Veslovsky went in the other.

It always went the same way with Levin: when his first shots failed, he got hot and out of temper, and shot badly the rest of the day. That was how it went today. There were plenty of snipe. They kept flying up from right under the dogs, from under the sportsmen's feet, and Levin might easily have made up for his bad start. But the more he shot, the more disgraced he felt in Veslovsky's eyes, as Veslovsky kept popping away merrily and indiscriminately, hitting nothing and not in the least troubled by his lack of success. Levin, hurrying feverishly, couldn't get a grip on himself, lost his temper more and more, and ended up firing with almost no real hope of hitting anything. Even Laska seemed to grasp it. She began searching more listlessly and would glance back at the sportsmen as if with puzzlement or reproach in her eyes. Shot after shot rang out. The smoke of the powder hung around the sportsmen, and yet in the wide, roomy net of the game bag there were only three little light snipe. And of those, one had been killed by Veslovsky alone, and one by both of them together. Meanwhile, from the other side of the marsh, came the sound of Stepan Arkadyevitch's shots — not frequent, but, as Levin imagined, well aimed, since after almost each one they heard "Krak, Krak, _apporte_!"

That excited Levin all the more. The snipe were floating constantly in the air above the reeds. The whir of wings near the ground and their harsh cries higher up could be heard on every side; the snipe that had risen first and shot up into the air were settling again right in front of the sportsmen. Instead of two hawks, there were now dozens of them hovering with shrill cries over the marsh.

After walking through more than half of the marsh, Levin and Veslovsky reached the point where the peasants' hayfield was divided into long strips running down to the reeds, marked off in one place by trampled grass, in another by a path mowed through it. Half the strips had already been cut.

Though there was less hope of finding birds in the uncut part than the cut part, Levin had promised Stepan Arkadyevitch to meet him at the mill, so he kept on with his companion across the cut and uncut patches.
"Hi there, sportsmen!" shouted one of a group of peasants sitting on an unharnessed cart. "Come and have some lunch with us! Have a drop of wine!"
Levin glanced around.
"Come on, it's all right!" shouted a good-humored, bearded peasant with a red face, showing his white teeth in a grin and holding up a greenish bottle that flashed in the sun.
"_Qu'est-ce qu'ils disent_?" asked Veslovsky.

"They're inviting you to have some vodka. They've probably been dividing the meadow into lots. I'd take some," Levin said, not without a touch of guile, hoping that Veslovsky would be tempted by the vodka and go off to them.
"Why are they offering it?"
"Oh, they're celebrating. Really, you should join them. You'd find it interesting."
"_Allons, c'est curieux_."

"Go on, go on — you'll find your way to the mill!" Levin called, and looking back he was glad to see Veslovsky, bent over and stumbling with weariness, his gun held out at arm's length, making his way out of the marsh toward the peasants.
"You come too!" the peasants shouted to Levin. "Don't be shy! Try our cake!"

Levin felt a strong urge for a drop of vodka and some bread. He was exhausted, and it took a real effort to drag his unsteady legs out of the mire, and for a moment he wavered. But Laska was on point. And immediately all his weariness vanished, and he walked lightly through the swamp toward the dog. A snipe flew up at his feet; he fired and killed it. Laska was still pointing. "Fetch it!" Another bird flew up close to the dog. Levin fired. But it was a bad day for him; he missed it, and when he went to look for the one he had shot, he couldn't find that one either. He wandered all through the reeds, but Laska did not believe he had shot it, and when he sent her to find it she only pretended to hunt, without really trying. And without Vassenka there for him to blame for his failure, things didn't go any better. There were still plenty of snipe, but Levin missed one after another.

The slanting rays of the sun were still hot; his clothes, soaked through with sweat, stuck to his body; his left boot, full of water, weighed down his leg and squeaked at every step; sweat trickled down his powder-blackened face; his mouth was full of a bitter taste, his nose of the smell of powder and stagnant water; his ears rang with the constant whir of snipe; he could not touch the stock of his gun, it had grown so hot; his heart beat in short, rapid throbs; his hands trembled with excitement, and his exhausted legs stumbled and lurched over the tussocks and through the marsh — and still he walked on and still he shot. At last, after one humiliating miss, he flung his gun and his hat down on the ground.

"No, I have to get a grip on myself," he said to himself. He picked up his gun and his hat, called Laska, and walked out of the swamp. When he reached dry ground he sat down, pulled off his boot and tipped it out, then walked over to the marsh, drank some stagnant-tasting water, wetted his burning-hot gun, and washed his face and hands. Refreshed, he went back to the spot where a snipe had landed, firmly determined to stay calm.
He tried to be calm, but it was the same all over again. His finger pressed the trigger before he had really aimed. It only got worse.
He had only five birds in his game bag when he walked out of the marsh toward the alders where he was to rejoin Stepan Arkadyevitch.

Before he caught sight of Stepan Arkadyevitch he spotted his dog. Krak shot out from behind the twisted root of an alder, black all over with the stinking mire of the marsh, and with the air of a victor sniffed at Laska. Behind Krak the well-built figure of Stepan Arkadyevitch came into view in the shade of the alder. He walked toward Levin, red and sweating, his collar unbuttoned, still limping in the same way.
"Well? You've been blazing away!" he said, smiling good-humoredly.
"And how did you do?" Levin asked. But there was no need to ask — he had already seen the full game bag.
"Oh, pretty fair."
He had fourteen birds.
"A splendid marsh! No doubt Veslovsky got in your way. It's awkward shooting with just one dog, too," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, to soften his triumph.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: When Levin and Stepan Arkadyevitch reached the peasant's hut where Levin always stayed, Veslovsky was already there. He was sitting in the middle of the room, gripping the bench with both hands while a soldier — the peasant's wife's brother — pulled him along by his mud-caked boots, trying to get them off. Veslovsky was laughing his infectious, good-humored laugh.

"I've only just gotten in. _Ils ont été charmants_. Just imagine — they gave me drink, fed me! Such bread, it was exquisite! _Délicieux!_ And the vodka, I never tasted any better. And they wouldn't take a penny for any of it. And they kept saying, 'Excuse our homely ways.'"

"What would they take anything for? They were treating you as a guest, of course. Do you suppose they keep vodka for sale?" the soldier said, finally getting the soaked boot off the blackened stocking.

In spite of the filth of the hut, all muddied by their boots and the dirty dogs licking themselves clean, and the smell of marsh slime and powder that filled the room, and the lack of knives and forks, the party drank their tea and ate their supper with a relish known only to sportsmen. Washed and clean, they then went into a hay barn that had been swept ready for them, where the coachman had been making up beds for the gentlemen.
Although it was already dusk, none of them wanted to go to sleep.

After drifting through reminiscences and anecdotes about guns, dogs, and former shooting parties, the conversation settled on a topic that interested all three of them. After Vassenka had several times expressed his admiration for this delightful sleeping place among the fragrant hay, this delightful broken cart (he had assumed it was broken because the shafts had been taken off), the good nature of the peasants who had treated him to vodka, and the dogs lying at their respective masters' feet, Oblonsky began telling them about a delightful shooting party at Malthus's that he had attended the previous summer.

Malthus was a well-known capitalist who had made his money speculating in railway shares. Stepan Arkadyevitch described what grouse moors this Malthus had bought up in the Tver province, how they were preserved, the carriages and dogcarts in which the shooting party had been driven about, and the luncheon pavilion that had been rigged up by the marsh.

"I don't understand you," said Levin, sitting up in the hay. "How is it that men like that don't disgust you? I can see that a lunch with Lafitte is all very pleasant, but don't you find that very lavishness distasteful? All those men, just like the old spirit monopolists in our day, make their money in a way that earns them everyone's contempt. They don't care about that contempt, and then they use their dishonest gains to buy off the contempt they have earned."
"Perfectly true!" chimed in Vassenka Veslovsky. "Perfectly! Oblonsky goes, of course, out of _bonhomie_, but other people say, 'Well, if Oblonsky stays with them...'"

"Not a bit of it." Levin could hear from Oblonsky's voice that he was smiling as he spoke. "I simply don't regard him as any more dishonest than any other rich merchant or aristocrat. They've all made their money in the same way — through their work and their intelligence."
"Oh, what kind of work? Do you call it work to get hold of concessions and then speculate with them?"
"Of course it's work. Work in the sense that if it weren't for him and others like him, there wouldn't be any railways."
"But it isn't work the way a peasant's work is work, or a scholar's."
"Granted, but it's work in the sense that his activity produces a result — the railways. Though of course you think railways are useless."
"No, that's a separate question; I'm willing to grant they're useful. But any profit that's out of all proportion to the labor that went into it is dishonest."
"But who's to say what's proportionate?"

"Profit made by dishonest means — by trickery," said Levin, aware that he could not draw a clean line between honesty and dishonesty. "Banking, for example," he went on. "It's an evil — the piling up of huge fortunes without labor, exactly the same thing as the old spirit monopolies; only the form has changed. _Le roi est mort, vive le roi_. No sooner had the spirit monopolies been abolished than along came the railways and the banking houses; that, too, is profit without work."

"Yes, that may all be very true and clever... Lie down, Krak!" Stepan Arkadyevitch called to his dog, who was scratching and turning over all the hay. He was clearly sure he was right, and so spoke calmly and without hurry. "But you haven't drawn the line between honest and dishonest work. The fact that I receive a bigger salary than my chief clerk, though he knows more about the work than I do — is that dishonest, in your view?"
"I can't say."

"Well, I'll tell you something: the fact that you receive, let's say, five thousand for your work on the land, while our host, the peasant here, no matter how hard he works, can never get more than fifty roubles, is just as dishonest as my earning more than my chief clerk, or Malthus's earning more than a stationmaster. No, on the contrary — I see that society takes a kind of hostile attitude toward these men, and it has no basis whatever; I suspect there's envy at the bottom of it..."
"No, that's not fair," said Veslovsky; "how can envy come into it? There's just something not right about that kind of business."
"You say," Levin went on, "that it's unjust for me to receive five thousand while the peasant gets fifty; that's true. It is unfair, and I feel it, but..."

"It really is. Why do we spend our days riding around, drinking, shooting, doing nothing, while they're always at work?" Vassenka Veslovsky said, evidently thinking the question through for the first time in his life and therefore considering it in perfect sincerity.
"Yes, you feel it, but you don't give him your property," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, deliberately, it seemed, to provoke Levin.

Lately a kind of quiet antagonism had grown up between the two brothers-in-law — as if, having married sisters, a sort of rivalry had sprung up between them over which of them was running his life better, and now that hostility was beginning to show in the conversation, which was taking on a personal edge.
"I don't give it away because nobody asks me to, and even if I wanted to, I couldn't give it away," Levin answered, "and I'd have no one to give it to."
"Give it to this peasant, he wouldn't say no."
"Yes, but how am I supposed to give it up? Am I to go to him and draw up a deed of conveyance?"
"I don't know; but if you're convinced you have no right to it..."
"I'm not at all convinced of that. On the contrary, I feel that I have no right to give it up — that I have duties both to the land and to my family."
"No, excuse me — if you think this inequality is unjust, why don't you act on it?..."
"Well, I do act on it negatively, in the sense that I don't try to widen the gap between him and me."
"No, excuse me, but that's a paradox."

"Yes, there's something of a sophistry about that," Veslovsky agreed. "Ah! our host — so you're not asleep yet?" he said to the peasant, who came into the barn just then, opening the creaking door. "How is it you're not asleep?"

"No, how could anyone sleep! I thought you gentlemen would be asleep already, but I heard you chattering. I came to get a hook from here. She won't bite?" he added, stepping cautiously in his bare feet.
"And where will you sleep?"
"We're going out for the night with the cattle."

"Ah, what a night!" said Veslovsky, looking out past the edge of the hut at the unharnessed wagonette, just visible in the faint light of the evening glow, framed by the open doors. "But listen — there are women's voices singing, and, my word, not badly either. Who's that singing, my friend?"
"That's the maids from just over there."
"Let's go, let's take a walk! We're not going to sleep anyway. Oblonsky, come on!"
"If only one could do both — lie here and go," Oblonsky answered, stretching. "It's wonderful lying here."

"Well, I'll go on my own then," said Veslovsky, getting up eagerly and pulling on his shoes and stockings. "Goodbye, gentlemen. If it's any fun, I'll come back for you. You've shown me some good sport, and I won't forget you."
"He really is a fine fellow, isn't he?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said when Veslovsky had gone out and the peasant had closed the door behind him.

"Yes, fine," Levin answered, still turning over the subject of their conversation in his mind. It seemed to him that he had spelled out his thoughts and feelings as clearly as he could, and yet both of these straightforward, no-fool men had said in the same breath that he was comforting himself with sophistries. That troubled him.

"It's just this, my dear boy. You have to do one of two things: either admit that the current order of society is just, and then defend your rights within it; or admit that you're enjoying unjust privileges, the way I do, and then enjoy them and be satisfied."
"No — if it were unjust, you couldn't enjoy those privileges and feel content; I at least couldn't. The main thing for me is to feel that I'm not to blame."
"What do you say, why don't we go after all?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, evidently tired of the strain of thinking. "We're not going to sleep, you know. Come on, let's go!"

Levin didn't answer. What they had said in the conversation — that he was being just only in a negative sense — kept turning in his mind. "Can it really be that one can only be just negatively?" he was asking himself.

"How strong the smell of the fresh hay is, though," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, getting up. "There's no chance of sleeping. Vassenka has been kicking up some fun out there. Do you hear the laughter, and his voice? Hadn't we better go? Come on!"
"No, I'm not coming," Levin answered.
"Surely that's not a matter of principle, too," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling, as he felt around in the dark for his cap.
"It's not a matter of principle, but why should I go?"
"You know you're storing up trouble for yourself," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, finding his cap and standing up.
"How so?"

"Do you think I haven't seen the line you've taken with your wife? I heard how it became a matter of the greatest importance whether you were to go away for a couple of days' shooting or not. That's all very well as a charming little episode, but as a rule for your whole life it won't do. A man has to be independent; he has his own masculine interests. A man has to be manly," said Oblonsky, opening the door.
"In what way? By chasing after servant girls?" said Levin.

"Why not, if it amuses him? _Ça ne tire pas à conséquence_. It does my wife no harm and it gives me a bit of fun. The main thing is to respect the sanctity of home. Nothing of the sort goes on at home. But don't tie your own hands."
"Perhaps," said Levin dryly, and he turned over on his side. "Tomorrow morning, early, I want to go shooting, and I won't wake anyone, and I'll be off at daybreak."

"_Messieurs, venez vite!_" they heard Veslovsky's voice coming back. "_Charmante!_ I've made such a discovery. _Charmante!_ A perfect Gretchen, and I've already made friends with her. Really, exceedingly pretty," he announced approvingly, as if she had been made pretty entirely for his benefit and he was now expressing his satisfaction with the entertainment provided for him.
Levin pretended to be asleep, while Oblonsky, putting on his slippers and lighting a cigar, walked out of the barn, and before long their voices died away.

For a long time Levin could not get to sleep. He heard the horses munching hay, then heard the peasant and his eldest boy getting ready and going out for the night watch with the cattle, then heard the soldier settling down on the other side of the barn with his nephew, the host's younger son. He heard the boy in his small, shrill voice telling his uncle what he thought about the dogs, who looked enormous and terrifying to him, asking what the dogs were going to hunt the next day, and the soldier answering in a hoarse, sleepy voice that the gentlemen were going to the marsh in the morning to shoot with their guns. Then, to put a stop to the boy's questions, he said, "Go to sleep, Vaska — go to sleep, or you'll catch it," and soon he himself began to snore, and everything fell still. He could hear only the snorting of the horses and the throaty cry of a snipe.
"Is it really only negative?" he repeated to himself. "Well, what of it? It isn't my fault." And he began thinking about the next day.

"Tomorrow I'll go out early, and I'll make a point of keeping cool. There are plenty of snipe, and grouse too. When I get back, there'll be the note from Kitty. Yes, Stiva may be right — I'm not manly with her, I'm tied to her apron strings... Well, it can't be helped! Negative again..."

Half asleep, he caught the laughter and the cheerful chatter of Veslovsky and Stepan Arkadyevitch. For a moment he opened his eyes: the moon was up, and in the doorway, brightly lit by the moonlight, the two of them were standing and talking. Stepan Arkadyevitch was saying something about the freshness of one of the girls, comparing her to a freshly peeled nut, and Veslovsky with his infectious laugh was repeating some line, probably said to him by a peasant: "Ah, you do your best to get round her!" Levin, half asleep, said:
"Gentlemen, tomorrow before dawn!" and fell asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Waking up at earliest dawn, Levin tried to wake his companions. Vassenka, lying on his stomach, with one leg in a stocking thrust out, was sleeping so soundly that he could elicit no response. Oblonsky, half asleep, declined to get up so early. Even Laska, who was asleep, curled up in the hay, got up unwillingly, and lazily stretched out and straightened her hind legs one after the other. Getting on his boots and stockings, taking his gun, and carefully opening the creaking door of the barn, Levin went out into the road. The coachmen were sleeping in their carriages, the horses were dozing. Only one was lazily eating oats, dipping its nose into the manger. It was still gray out-of-doors.
"Why are you up so early, my dear?" the old woman, their hostess, said, coming out of the hut and addressing him affectionately as an old friend.
"Going shooting, granny. Do I go this way to the marsh?"

"Straight out at the back; by our threshing floor, my dear, and hemp patches; there's a little footpath." Stepping carefully with her sunburnt, bare feet, the old woman conducted Levin, and moved back the fence for him by the threshing floor.
"Straight on and you'll come to the marsh. Our lads drove the cattle there yesterday evening."

Laska ran eagerly forward along the little path. Levin followed her with a light, rapid step, continually looking at the sky. He hoped the sun would not be up before he reached the marsh. But the sun did not delay. The moon, which had been bright when he went out, by now shone only like a crescent of quicksilver. The pink flush of dawn, which one could not help seeing before, now had to be sought to be discerned at all. What were before undefined, vague blurs in the distant countryside could now be distinctly seen. They were sheaves of rye. The dew, not visible till the sun was up, wetted Levin's legs and his blouse above his belt in the high growing, fragrant hemp patch, from which the pollen had already fallen out. In the transparent stillness of morning the smallest sounds were audible. A bee flew by Levin's ear with the whizzing sound of a bullet. He looked carefully, and saw a second and a third. They were all flying from the beehives behind the hedge, and they disappeared over the hemp patch in the direction of the marsh. The path led straight to the marsh. The marsh could be recognized by the mist which rose from it, thicker in one place and thinner in another, so that the reeds and willow bushes swayed like islands in this mist. At the edge of the marsh and the road, peasant boys and men, who had been herding for the night, were lying, and in the dawn all were asleep under their coats. Not far from them were three hobbled horses. One of them clanked a chain. Laska walked beside her master, pressing a little forward and looking round. Passing the sleeping peasants and reaching the first reeds, Levin examined his pistols and let his dog off. One of the horses, a sleek, dark-brown three-year-old, seeing the dog, started away, switched its tail and snorted. The other horses too were frightened, and splashing through the water with their hobbled legs, and drawing their hoofs out of the thick mud with a squelching sound, they bounded out of the marsh. Laska stopped, looking ironically at the horses and inquiringly at Levin. Levin patted Laska, and whistled as a sign that she might begin.
Laska ran joyfully and anxiously through the slush that swayed under her.

Running into the marsh among the familiar scents of roots, marsh plants, and slime, and the extraneous smell of horse dung, Laska detected at once a smell that pervaded the whole marsh, the scent of that strong-smelling bird that always excited her more than any other. Here and there among the moss and marsh plants this scent was very strong, but it was impossible to determine in which direction it grew stronger or fainter. To find the direction, she had to go farther away from the wind. Not feeling the motion of her legs, Laska bounded with a stiff gallop, so that at each bound she could stop short, to the right, away from the wind that blew from the east before sunrise, and turned facing the wind. Sniffing in the air with dilated nostrils, she felt at once that not their tracks only but they themselves were here before her, and not one, but many. Laska slackened her speed. They were here, but where precisely she could not yet determine. To find the very spot, she began to make a circle, when suddenly her master's voice drew her off. "Laska! here?" he asked, pointing her to a different direction. She stopped, asking him if she had better not go on doing as she had begun. But he repeated his command in an angry voice, pointing to a spot covered with water, where there could not be anything. She obeyed him, pretending she was looking, so as to please him, went round it, and went back to her former position, and was at once aware of the scent again. Now when he was not hindering her, she knew what to do, and without looking at what was under her feet, and to her vexation stumbling over a high stump into the water, but righting herself with her strong, supple legs, she began making the circle which was to make all clear to her. The scent of them reached her, stronger and stronger, and more and more defined, and all at once it became perfectly clear to her that one of them was here, behind this tuft of reeds, five paces in front of her; she stopped, and her whole body was still and rigid. On her short legs she could see nothing in front of her, but by the scent she knew it was sitting not more than five paces off. She stood still, feeling more and more conscious of it, and enjoying it in anticipation. Her tail was stretched straight and tense, and only wagging at the extreme end. Her mouth was slightly open, her ears raised. One ear had been turned wrong side out as she ran up, and she breathed heavily but warily, and still more warily looked round, but more with her eyes than her head, to her master. He was coming along with the face she knew so well, though the eyes were always terrible to her. He stumbled over the stump as he came, and moved, as she thought, extraordinarily slowly. She thought he came slowly, but he was running.

Noticing Laska's special attitude as she crouched on the ground, as it were, scratching big prints with her hind paws, and with her mouth slightly open, Levin knew she was pointing at grouse, and with an inward prayer for luck, especially with the first bird, he ran up to her. Coming quite close up to her, he could from his height look beyond her, and he saw with his eyes what she was seeing with her nose. In a space between two little thickets, at a couple of yards' distance, he could see a grouse. Turning its head, it was listening. Then lightly preening and folding its wings, it disappeared round a corner with a clumsy wag of its tail.
"Fetch it, fetch it!" shouted Levin, giving Laska a shove from behind.

"But I can't go," thought Laska. "Where am I to go? From here I feel them, but if I move forward I shall know nothing of where they are or who they are." But then he shoved her with his knee, and in an excited whisper said, "Fetch it, Laska."

"Well, if that's what he wishes, I'll do it, but I can't answer for myself now," she thought, and darted forward as fast as her legs would carry her between the thick bushes. She scented nothing now; she could only see and hear, without understanding anything.

Ten paces from her former place a grouse rose with a guttural cry and the peculiar round sound of its wings. And immediately after the shot it splashed heavily with its white breast on the wet mire. Another bird did not linger, but rose behind Levin without the dog. When Levin turned towards it, it was already some way off. But his shot caught it. Flying twenty paces further, the second grouse rose upwards, and whirling round like a ball, dropped heavily on a dry place.
"Come, this is going to be some good!" thought Levin, packing the warm and fat grouse into his game bag. "Eh, Laska, will it be good?"

When Levin, after loading his gun, moved on, the sun had fully risen, though unseen behind the storm-clouds. The moon had lost all of its luster, and was like a white cloud in the sky. Not a single star could be seen. The sedge, silvery with dew before, now shone like gold. The stagnant pools were all like amber. The blue of the grass had changed to yellow-green. The marsh birds twittered and swarmed about the brook and upon the bushes that glittered with dew and cast long shadows. A hawk woke up and settled on a haycock, turning its head from side to side and looking discontentedly at the marsh. Crows were flying about the field, and a bare-legged boy was driving the horses to an old man, who had got up from under his long coat and was combing his hair. The smoke from the gun was white as milk over the green of the grass.
One of the boys ran up to Levin.
"Uncle, there were ducks here yesterday!" he shouted to him, and he walked a little way off behind him.
And Levin was doubly pleased, in sight of the boy, who expressed his approval, at killing three snipe, one after another, straight off.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: The sportsman's saying, that if the first beast or the first bird is not missed, the day will be lucky, turned out correct.

At ten o'clock Levin, weary, hungry, and happy after a tramp of twenty miles, returned to his night's lodging with nineteen head of fine game and one duck, which he tied to his belt, as it would not go into the game bag. His companions had long been awake, and had had time to get hungry and have breakfast.

"Wait a bit, wait a bit, I know there are nineteen," said Levin, counting a second time over the grouse and snipe, that looked so much less important now, bent and dry and bloodstained, with heads crooked aside, than they did when they were flying.
The number was verified, and Stepan Arkadyevitch's envy pleased Levin. He was pleased too on returning to find the man sent by Kitty with a note was already there.

"I am perfectly well and happy. If you were uneasy about me, you can feel easier than ever. I've a new bodyguard, Marya Vlasyevna,"—this was the midwife, a new and important personage in Levin's domestic life. "She has come to have a look at me. She found me perfectly well, and we have kept her till you are back. All are happy and well, and please, don't be in a hurry to come back, but, if the sport is good, stay another day."

These two pleasures, his lucky shooting and the letter from his wife, were so great that two slightly disagreeable incidents passed lightly over Levin. One was that the chestnut trace horse, who had been unmistakably overworked on the previous day, was off his feed and out of sorts. The coachman said he was "Overdriven yesterday, Konstantin Dmitrievitch. Yes, indeed! driven ten miles with no sense!"

The other unpleasant incident, which for the first minute destroyed his good humor, though later he laughed at it a great deal, was to find that of all the provisions Kitty had provided in such abundance that one would have thought there was enough for a week, nothing was left. On his way back, tired and hungry from shooting, Levin had so distinct a vision of meat-pies that as he approached the hut he seemed to smell and taste them, as Laska had smelt the game, and he immediately told Philip to give him some. It appeared that there were no pies left, nor even any chicken.
"Well, this fellow's appetite!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, laughing and pointing at Vassenka Veslovsky. "I never suffer from loss of appetite, but he's really marvelous!..."
"Well, it can't be helped," said Levin, looking gloomily at Veslovsky. "Well, Philip, give me some beef, then."
"The beef's been eaten, and the bones given to the dogs," answered Philip.
Levin was so hurt that he said, in a tone of vexation, "You might have left me something!" and he felt ready to cry.
"Then put away the game," he said in a shaking voice to Philip, trying not to look at Vassenka, "and cover them with some nettles. And you might at least ask for some milk for me."
But when he had drunk some milk, he felt ashamed immediately at having shown his annoyance to a stranger, and he began to laugh at his hungry mortification.
In the evening they went shooting again, and Veslovsky had several successful shots, and in the night they drove home.

Their homeward journey was as lively as their drive out had been. Veslovsky sang songs and related with enjoyment his adventures with the peasants, who had regaled him with vodka, and said to him, "Excuse our homely ways," and his night's adventures with kiss-in-the-ring and the servant-girl and the peasant, who had asked him was he married, and on learning that he was not, said to him, "Well, mind you don't run after other men's wives—you'd better get one of your own." These words had particularly amused Veslovsky.
"Altogether, I've enjoyed our outing awfully. And you, Levin?"

"I have, very much," Levin said quite sincerely. It was particularly delightful to him to have got rid of the hostility he had been feeling towards Vassenka Veslovsky at home, and to feel instead the most friendly disposition to him.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Next day at ten o'clock Levin, who had already gone his rounds, knocked at the room where Vassenka had been put for the night.
"_Entrez!_" Veslovsky called to him. "Excuse me, I've only just finished my ablutions," he said, smiling, standing before him in his underclothes only.
"Don't mind me, please." Levin sat down in the window. "Have you slept well?"
"Like the dead. What sort of day is it for shooting?"
"What will you take, tea or coffee?"
"Neither. I'll wait till lunch. I'm really ashamed. I suppose the ladies are down? A walk now would be capital. You show me your horses."

After walking about the garden, visiting the stable, and even doing some gymnastic exercises together on the parallel bars, Levin returned to the house with his guest, and went with him into the drawing-room.
"We had splendid shooting, and so many delightful experiences!" said Veslovsky, going up to Kitty, who was sitting at the samovar. "What a pity ladies are cut off from these delights!"
"Well, I suppose he must say something to the lady of the house," Levin said to himself. Again he fancied something in the smile, in the all-conquering air with which their guest addressed Kitty....

The princess, sitting on the other side of the table with Marya Vlasyevna and Stepan Arkadyevitch, called Levin to her side, and began to talk to him about moving to Moscow for Kitty's confinement, and getting ready rooms for them. Just as Levin had disliked all the trivial preparations for his wedding, as derogatory to the grandeur of the event, now he felt still more offensive the preparations for the approaching birth, the date of which they reckoned, it seemed, on their fingers. He tried to turn a deaf ear to these discussions of the best patterns of long clothes for the coming baby; tried to turn away and avoid seeing the mysterious, endless strips of knitting, the triangles of linen, and so on, to which Dolly attached special importance. The birth of a son (he was certain it would be a son) which was promised him, but which he still could not believe in—so marvelous it seemed—presented itself to his mind, on one hand, as a happiness so immense, and therefore so incredible; on the other, as an event so mysterious, that this assumption of a definite knowledge of what would be, and consequent preparation for it, as for something ordinary that did happen to people, jarred on him as confusing and humiliating.

But the princess did not understand his feelings, and put down his reluctance to think and talk about it to carelessness and indifference, and so she gave him no peace. She had commissioned Stepan Arkadyevitch to look at a flat, and now she called Levin up.
"I know nothing about it, princess. Do as you think fit," he said.
"You must decide when you will move."
"I really don't know. I know millions of children are born away from Moscow, and doctors ... why...."
"But if so...."
"Oh, no, as Kitty wishes."
"We can't talk to Kitty about it! Do you want me to frighten her? Why, this spring Natalia Golitzina died from having an ignorant doctor."
"I will do just what you say," he said gloomily.

The princess began talking to him, but he did not hear her. Though the conversation with the princess had indeed jarred upon him, he was gloomy, not on account of that conversation, but from what he saw at the samovar.
"No, it's impossible," he thought, glancing now and then at Vassenka bending over Kitty, telling her something with his charming smile, and at her, flushed and disturbed.

There was something not nice in Vassenka's attitude, in his eyes, in his smile. Levin even saw something not nice in Kitty's attitude and look. And again the light died away in his eyes. Again, as before, all of a sudden, without the slightest transition, he felt cast down from a pinnacle of happiness, peace, and dignity, into an abyss of despair, rage, and humiliation. Again everything and everyone had become hateful to him.
"You do just as you think best, princess," he said again, looking round.
"Heavy is the cap of Monomach," Stepan Arkadyevitch said playfully, hinting, evidently, not simply at the princess's conversation, but at the cause of Levin's agitation, which he had noticed.
"How late you are today, Dolly!"

Everyone got up to greet Darya Alexandrovna. Vassenka only rose for an instant, and with the lack of courtesy to ladies characteristic of the modern young man, he scarcely bowed, and resumed his conversation again, laughing at something.
"I've been worried about Masha. She did not sleep well, and is dreadfully tiresome today," said Dolly.

The conversation Vassenka had started with Kitty was running on the same lines as on the previous evening, discussing Anna, and whether love is to be put higher than worldly considerations. Kitty disliked the conversation, and she was disturbed both by the subject and the tone in which it was conducted, and also by the knowledge of the effect it would have on her husband. But she was too simple and innocent to know how to cut short this conversation, or even to conceal the superficial pleasure afforded her by the young man's very obvious admiration. She wanted to stop it, but she did not know what to do. Whatever she did she knew would be observed by her husband, and the worst interpretation put on it. And, in fact, when she asked Dolly what was wrong with Masha, and Vassenka, waiting till this uninteresting conversation was over, began to gaze indifferently at Dolly, the question struck Levin as an unnatural and disgusting piece of hypocrisy.
"What do you say, shall we go and look for mushrooms today?" said Dolly.

"By all means, please, and I shall come too," said Kitty, and she blushed. She wanted from politeness to ask Vassenka whether he would come, and she did not ask him. "Where are you going, Kostya?" she asked her husband with a guilty face, as he passed by her with a resolute step. This guilty air confirmed all his suspicions.
"The mechanician came when I was away; I haven't seen him yet," he said, not looking at her.
He went downstairs, but before he had time to leave his study he heard his wife's familiar footsteps running with reckless speed to him.
"What do you want?" he said to her shortly. "We are busy."
"I beg your pardon," she said to the German mechanician; "I want a few words with my husband."
The German would have left the room, but Levin said to him:
"Don't disturb yourself."
"The train is at three?" queried the German. "I mustn't be late."
Levin did not answer him, but walked out himself with his wife.
"Well, what have you to say to me?" he said to her in French.
He did not look her in the face, and did not care to see that she in her condition was trembling all over, and had a piteous, crushed look.
"I ... I want to say that we can't go on like this; that this is misery...." she said.
"The servants are here at the sideboard," he said angrily; "don't make a scene."
"Well, let's go in here!"
They were standing in the passage. Kitty would have gone into the next room, but there the English governess was giving Tanya a lesson.
"Well, come into the garden."

In the garden they came upon a peasant weeding the path. And no longer considering that the peasant could see her tear-stained and his agitated face, that they looked like people fleeing from some disaster, they went on with rapid steps, feeling that they must speak out and clear up misunderstandings, must be alone together, and so get rid of the misery they were both feeling.
"We can't go on like this! It's misery! I am wretched; you are wretched. What for?" she said, when they had at last reached a solitary garden seat at a turn in the lime tree avenue.

"But tell me one thing: was there in his tone anything unseemly, not nice, humiliatingly horrible?" he said, standing before her again in the same position with his clenched fists on his chest, as he had stood before her that night.

"Yes," she said in a shaking voice; "but, Kostya, surely you see I'm not to blame? All the morning I've been trying to take a tone ... but such people.... Why did he come? How happy we were!" she said, breathless with the sobs that shook her.

Although nothing had been pursuing them, and there was nothing to run away from, and they could not possibly have found anything very delightful on that garden seat, the gardener saw with astonishment that they passed him on their way home with comforted and radiant faces.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: After escorting his wife upstairs, Levin went to Dolly's part of the house. Darya Alexandrovna, for her part, was in great distress too that day. She was walking about the room, talking angrily to a little girl, who stood in the corner roaring.
"And you shall stand all day in the corner, and have your dinner all alone, and not see one of your dolls, and I won't make you a new frock," she said, not knowing how to punish her.
"Oh, she is a disgusting child!" she turned to Levin. "Where does she get such wicked propensities?"
"Why, what has she done?" Levin said without much interest, for he had wanted to ask her advice, and so was annoyed that he had come at an unlucky moment.

"Grisha and she went into the raspberries, and there ... I can't tell you really what she did. It's a thousand pities Miss Elliot's not with us. This one sees to nothing—she's a machine.... _Figurez-vous que la petite_?..."
And Darya Alexandrovna described Masha's crime.
"That proves nothing; it's not a question of evil propensities at all, it's simply mischief," Levin assured her.
"But you are upset about something? What have you come for?" asked Dolly. "What's going on there?"
And in the tone of her question Levin heard that it would be easy for him to say what he had meant to say.
"I've not been in there, I've been alone in the garden with Kitty. We've had a quarrel for the second time since ... Stiva came."
Dolly looked at him with her shrewd, comprehending eyes.
"Come, tell me, honor bright, has there been ... not in Kitty, but in that gentleman's behavior, a tone which might be unpleasant—not unpleasant, but horrible, offensive to a husband?"

"You mean, how shall I say.... Stay, stay in the corner!" she said to Masha, who, detecting a faint smile in her mother's face, had been turning round. "The opinion of the world would be that he is behaving as young men do behave. _Il fait la cour à une jeune et jolie femme_, and a husband who's a man of the world should only be flattered by it."
"Yes, yes," said Levin gloomily; "but you noticed it?"
"Not only I, but Stiva noticed it. Just after breakfast he said to me in so many words, _Je crois que Veslovsky fait un petit brin de cour à Kitty_."
"Well, that's all right then; now I'm satisfied. I'll send him away," said Levin.

"What do you mean! Are you crazy?" Dolly cried in horror; "nonsense, Kostya, only think!" she said, laughing. "You can go now to Fanny," she said to Masha. "No, if you wish it, I'll speak to Stiva. He'll take him away. He can say you're expecting visitors. Altogether he doesn't fit into the house."
"No, no, I'll do it myself."
"But you'll quarrel with him?"

"Not a bit. I shall so enjoy it," Levin said, his eyes flashing with real enjoyment. "Come, forgive her, Dolly, she won't do it again," he said of the little sinner, who had not gone to Fanny, but was standing irresolutely before her mother, waiting and looking up from under her brows to catch her mother's eye.
The mother glanced at her. The child broke into sobs, hid her face on her mother's lap, and Dolly laid her thin, tender hand on her head.
"And what is there in common between us and him?" thought Levin, and he went off to look for Veslovsky.
As he passed through the passage he gave orders for the carriage to be got ready to drive to the station.
"The spring was broken yesterday," said the footman.
"Well, the covered trap, then, and make haste. Where's the visitor?"
"The gentleman's gone to his room."
Levin came upon Veslovsky at the moment when the latter, having unpacked his things from his trunk, and laid out some new songs, was putting on his gaiters to go out riding.

Whether there was something exceptional in Levin's face, or that Vassenka was himself conscious that _ce petit brin de cour_ he was making was out of place in this family, but he was somewhat (as much as a young man in society can be) disconcerted at Levin's entrance.
"You ride in gaiters?"
"Yes, it's much cleaner," said Vassenka, putting his fat leg on a chair, fastening the bottom hook, and smiling with simple-hearted good humor.
He was undoubtedly a good-natured fellow, and Levin felt sorry for him and ashamed of himself, as his host, when he saw the shy look on Vassenka's face.

On the table lay a piece of stick which they had broken together that morning, trying their strength. Levin took the fragment in his hands and began smashing it up, breaking bits off the stick, not knowing how to begin.
"I wanted...." He paused, but suddenly, remembering Kitty and everything that had happened, he said, looking him resolutely in the face: "I have ordered the horses to be put-to for you."
"How so?" Vassenka began in surprise. "To drive where?"
"For you to drive to the station," Levin said gloomily.
"Are you going away, or has something happened?"

"It happens that I expect visitors," said Levin, his strong fingers more and more rapidly breaking off the ends of the split stick. "And I'm not expecting visitors, and nothing has happened, but I beg you to go away. You can explain my rudeness as you like."
Vassenka drew himself up.
"I beg you to explain...." he said with dignity, understanding at last.
"I can't explain," Levin said softly and deliberately, trying to control the trembling of his jaw; "and you'd better not ask."
And as the split ends were all broken off, Levin clutched the thick ends in his finger, broke the stick in two, and carefully caught the end as it fell.

Probably the sight of those nervous fingers, of the muscles he had proved that morning at gymnastics, of the glittering eyes, the soft voice, and quivering jaws, convinced Vassenka better than any words. He bowed, shrugging his shoulders, and smiling contemptuously.
"Can I not see Oblonsky?"
The shrug and the smile did not irritate Levin.
"What else was there for him to do?" he thought.
"I'll send him to you at once."

"What madness is this?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said when, after hearing from his friend that he was being turned out of the house, he found Levin in the garden, where he was walking about waiting for his guest's departure. "_Mais c'est ridicule!_ What fly has stung you? _Mais c'est du dernier ridicule!_ What did you think, if a young man...."
But the place where Levin had been stung was evidently still sore, for he turned pale again, when Stepan Arkadyevitch would have enlarged on the reason, and he himself cut him short.

"Please don't go into it! I can't help it. I feel ashamed of how I'm treating you and him. But it won't be, I imagine, a great grief to him to go, and his presence was distasteful to me and to my wife."
"But it's insulting to him! _Et puis c'est ridicule_."
"And to me it's both insulting and distressing! And I'm not at fault in any way, and there's no need for me to suffer."
"Well, this I didn't expect of you! _On peut être jaloux, mais à ce point, c'est du dernier ridicule!_"

Levin turned quickly, and walked away from him into the depths of the avenue, and he went on walking up and down alone. Soon he heard the rumble of the trap, and saw from behind the trees how Vassenka, sitting in the hay (unluckily there was no seat in the trap) in his Scotch cap, was driven along the avenue, jolting up and down over the ruts.

"What's this?" Levin thought, when a footman ran out of the house and stopped the trap. It was the mechanician, whom Levin had totally forgotten. The mechanician, bowing low, said something to Veslovsky, then clambered into the trap, and they drove off together.

Stepan Arkadyevitch and the princess were much upset by Levin's action. And he himself felt not only in the highest degree _ridicule_, but also utterly guilty and disgraced. But remembering what sufferings he and his wife had been through, when he asked himself how he should act another time, he answered that he should do just the same again.

In spite of all this, towards the end of that day, everyone except the princess, who could not pardon Levin's action, became extraordinarily lively and good-humored, like children after a punishment or grown-up people after a dreary, ceremonious reception, so that by the evening Vassenka's dismissal was spoken of, in the absence of the princess, as though it were some remote event.
